item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — In the end, the unfamiliarity outshined the shock.
The defeated 2026 Los Angeles Dodgers, many of them back-to-back champs, hadn't been forced to face this uncomfortable silence in a while. A four-game drubbing courtesy of the Milwaukee Brewers in a stunningly comprehensive NLCS sweep cast onto the most expensive team ever assembled a very foreign feeling: failure.
Milwaukee, so often bounced early in the October melee, knows that discomfort and its soundtrack. That unsettling hush that comes with the humbling unmooring of a premature postseason exit. Hugs, daps, thank yous, low-volume answers, goodbyes, regrets. But here it was, here the Dodgers were, in the tricked-out home clubhouse grappling with the end of something.
On one side of the room, Shohei Ohtani stood in front of his locker before a massive semicircle of reporters and TV cameras. For the first time in his MLB career, he'd lost a postseason series. His signing with L.A. ahead of the 2024 season sparked this era of supercharged dominance. And for eight October series his Dodgers were untouchable. Usually, during this spot in the calendar, Ohtani is getting drenched in imitation champagne as Latin rap and joyous roars echo in the background.
The scene Thursday night was a drier, quieter experience.
Join or create a Yahoo Fantasy Basketball league for the 2026-27 NBA season
This seemingly indomitable baseball behemoth donned street clothes and a New Balance backward cap, small beads of sweat still pooling on his face, trying to explain what went wrong and where he goes from here.
"I haven't been able to really come to grips in terms of what I've learned overall this season," Ohtani said via interpreter Will Ireton. "I'm going to go back to the drawing board in terms of treatment, training program and see what I can come up with next season."
The postmortem on Los Angeles' crash-out can be as extensive as you choose to make it. But simply put, they were the inferior team. Slower, older, colder and less fearsome than the hard-charging Brewers. Baseball's most aged offense failed to slug and didn't perform with runners in scoring position. One of the most talented rotations ever assembled wasn't dominant enough to make up the difference.
All season, the Dodgers touted their experience as a calling card. Perhaps, if the series had been closer, that might have mattered. As it stands, it's less necessary to assign blame when so much went wrong.
"I think for me, it never feels good to lose, but when you get beat, you can handle it a little bit better," manager Dave Roberts said after his team's 6-4 loss in Game 4.
The morning after, fans across the baseball universe are celebrating the Dodgers' downfall. They aren't the only ones. As Milwaukee's champagne celebration roared in the visiting clubhouse, Brewers coaches and executives were already receiving texts of appreciation and congratulations on slaying the mighty dragon.
But don't expect the upcoming small-market Fall Classic to remedy baseball's impending labor struggle. With the current collective bargaining agreement set to expire on Dec. 1, the league and the owners have been pushing hard for the adoption of a salary cap. Certainly, that argument becomes at least somewhat trickier to make with the half-billion-dollar boogeyman Dodgers on vacation, but the league won't suddenly change course after four games. The showdown over a cap was always going to be drawn-out and messy, no matter which team is the last one standing.
For the Dodgers organization, the uncertainty about baseball's future further complicates what was always going to be a critical offseason. One October exit won't kill off this juggernaut. Neither will a new economic landscape. The Dodgers remain advantageously positioned to compete for championships over the next decade and beyond. That's a testament to both their player-development prowess and their imposing spending power.
But the questions are already piling on Andrew Friedman's desk. Surely, the president of baseball operations is already considering the future and how this winter will shape the 2027 Dodgers.
No task is more important than figuring out what went wrong with Ohtani's season. For three months, the two-way star was, for the first time as a Dodger, doing full two-way stardom. Another MVP felt like an inevitability. Then his biceps started barking. A start on the mound was pushed back, then scratched, then so was another. Ohtani didn't throw a single in-game pitch after July 3.
His attempts to get back on the mound then appeared to compromise his offensive talents. He got ice-cold in late August into September. His physicality began to fray. His body wasn't right. Eventually, the Dodgers had no choice but to place him on the injured list. Only over the last two days of the Dodgers' postseason did Ohtani look anything like himself.
Communication with the four-time MVP has rarely been perfect. Some of that is the language barrier. Some of that is Ohtani's lone ranger approach. But now both sides need to evaluate why a diminished version of Ohtani was forced to play through pain. After the Game 4 loss, Ohtani told reporters that he intends to pitch next season. In what capacity remains to be seen. It might behoove the Dodgers to slow-play his recovery timeline to ensure he's available when they need him most — in the postseason.
There are a mountain of transactional questions as well. Tarik Skubal, added in a deadline blockbuster, is now a free agent. Will the Dodgers flex their muscles to re-sign him? Or do they want to give younger arms such as Roki Sasaki, Emmet Sheehan and Justin Wrobleski some rotation runway? What about upper-level pitching prospects such as Christian Zazueta, Zach Root, Adam Serwinowski and Jackson Ferris? Could they let Skubal walk in favor of a different free-agent starter? Freddy Peralta has looked pretty good recently.
Positionally, though, is where Los Angeles' bigger roster-construction conversations will take place. They got mollywhopped by Milwaukee in part because the Dodgers' offense looked unathletic and elderly. Friedman has expressed a desire to inject more youth into the group, but that's easier said than done. A number of spots feel set in stone: Ohtani at DH, Will Smith at catcher, Freddie Freeman at first, Mookie Betts at short, Kyle Tucker in right field, Andy Pages in center.
Max Muncy (3B) and Teoscar Hernández (LF) are older players expected to reach free agency after 2027. A trade of either could be a way to reshuffle the deck, with Hernández the likelier to go. Tommy Edman had a second straight mediocre, injury-marred campaign, but he has four seasons left on his contract. Might the Dodgers seek a suitor for the switch-hitting utilityman?
Even after harvesting the farm for the Skubal trade, Los Angeles has one of the most stocked systems in the sport. Most of their prospect juice is concentrated in the outfield. Five Dodgers outfield prospects at Double-A or above — Josue De Paula, Eduardo Quintero, Mike Sirota, Charles Davalan and James Tibbs III — could find themselves on offseason top-100 lists. De Paula, who impressed in a late-season cup of coffee, Quintero and Sirota are currently ranked fourth, 15th and 17th, respectively, by MLB Pipeline.
Unfortunately for the Dodgers, you can play only three outfielders at a time. In their existing outfield, they already have the highest-paid player in the sport (Tucker) and the starting center fielder in the 2026 All-Star Game (Pages). With just one spot remaining, it'll be fascinating to see how Friedman makes use of his farm system.
For the players, none of these contingencies or scenarios will offer any short-term solace. They aimed for a three-peat and missed. That sting will take time to subside, even if the 2027 Dodgers project to be a similarly formidable force.
"We fell short, you know?" utilityman Kiké Hernández lamented postgame. "We had a good run, but here we are."

item.title: [New York Post] Mookie Betts sends heartfelt message to Dodgers fans after Brewers sweep in NLCS
item.dc:creator: Valentina Martinez
item.description: Less than 24 hours after the Dodgers were swept by the Brewers in the National League Championship Series, Mookie Betts addressed the fanbase. “This season didn’t end the way we wanted, but I just want to say thank you to everyone who supported us along the way,” the Dodgers shortstop wrote in an Instagram post. “Through the ups and downs, you continued to show up and show love. I don’t take any of that for granted. Thank you, Dodger Nation.” The Dodgers’ season came to an untimely end on Thursd
item.content:encoded:
Less than 24 hours after the Dodgers were swept by the Brewers in the National League Championship Series, Mookie Betts addressed the fanbase.
“This season didn’t end the way we wanted, but I just want to say thank you to everyone who supported us along the way,” the Dodgers shortstop wrote in an Instagram post.
“Through the ups and downs, you continued to show up and show love. I don’t take any of that for granted. Thank you, Dodger Nation.”
The Dodgers’ season came to an untimely end on Thursday night as the Brewers were awarded the National League pennant after a dominant four-game performance over the back-to-back World Series champions.
The Dodgers assembled one of the greatest rosters in baseball and spared no expense to do so. But the NLCS proved that while the Dodgers may be the richest team in the league, luxurious spending does not guarantee a championship.
Now, the juggernaut will be forced to evaluate how to approach the upcoming 2027 season. Will Shohei Ohtani pitch again? Should the Dodgers trade Teoscar Hernandez or Tommy Edman? Will free agent Tarik Skubal be back in LA? How do the Dodgers get younger?
All those questions and more will have to be addressed this winter as the Dodgers dynasty looks to recover from a failed three-peat attempt.
While the team ultimately fell short in 2026, there’s a chance the Dodgers could very well make another deep playoff run next year if the front office can assemble all the right pieces.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] What Dave Roberts Said After Dodgers Season Ended (And What it Means for This Offseason)
item.dc:creator: Gabe Smallson; Unknown
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers were swept by the Milwaukee Brewers in the National League Championship Series and now face a long offseason. Manager Dave Roberts recently came under fire for a few questionable decisions during Game 3's loss, and his response was reshuffling the lineup to a more familiar look than the last contest. Shohei Ohtani was back in his leadoff spot, and after an Andy Pages RBI single in the second inning, appeared to validate Roberts' move with a three-run home run to take a co
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers were swept by the Milwaukee Brewers in the National League Championship Series and now face a long offseason.
Manager Dave Roberts recently came under fire for a few questionable decisions during Game 3's loss, and his response was reshuffling the lineup to a more familiar look than the last contest. Shohei Ohtani was back in his leadoff spot, and after an Andy Pages RBI single in the second inning, appeared to validate Roberts' move with a three-run home run to take a commanding 4-0 lead.
For just a moment, it appeared that the two-time defending champions would force a Game 5 with two-time Cy Young award winner Tarik Skubal on the mound. Unfortunately, this lasted just two frames.
Though baseball fans are able to point to many moments these past four games that reflected poorly on a Roberts decision, the offense was inexcusable all series long. During the regular season, the Dodgers hit .257 (third in MLB), but over the course of the NLCS, hit just .187.
Despite the output, nothing could change how the skipper felt about his group. Roberts spoke after the contest on how proud he is of his team.
"Extremely proud," Robert said. "It never feels good to lose and not accomplish a goal to win the World Series. It started back in the early part of February. I love this team and what we had to go through. It’s one of those things that every night we take the field, people are bringing their best to beat us."
Going into the NLCS, the Dodgers had a roster with the average age of 30.9 years old (the oldest in MLB) to the Brewers' average age of 27.3 (the 12th youngest). Roberts was asked about the factor that age played in this series, and had a response that is very telling for the team's offseason plans.
"I really appreciate the question. I just don’t think that in four games that we came up short that age was a factor," Roberts said. "What I will say is that those guys, some of the plays that [Brice] Turang made going to his right, the plays that the outfielders made, that’s certainly youth and talent.
It wasn’t that they were fatigued. We have off days going into series. I just don’t think that our age of our ball club reflected this series. We got beat.
"There’s no because we’re too old or whatever. Every facet of the game, if you kind of unpack it, we were bested."
Roberts' unwavering support of his veterans will likely enhance the trust in the clubhouse, and with a long offseason now underway, will hopefully translate into regrouping and retooling for 2027.

Gabe Smallson is a sportswriter based in Los Angeles with a focus in sports and entertainment content. Gabe has previously worked at Newsweek and Dodgers Nation. He graduated from San Francisco State University in 2020 and received his Masters of Science at the University of Southern California in 2025.

item.dc:creator: Jackson Kruse
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers acquired left-hander Tarik Skubal from the Detroit Tigers last summer, hoping he could help the team three-peat as World Series champions. The Dodgers officially won’t reach their goal after being swept by the Milwaukee Brewers 4-0 in the National League Championship Series. Skubal is now officially a free agent. After the Brewers completed the sweep at Dodger Stadium on Thursday night, Skubal addressed his future. Ex-Detroit Tigers LHP Tarik Skubal Makes Statement on Fre
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers acquired left-hander Tarik Skubal from the Detroit Tigers last summer, hoping he could help the team three-peat as World Series champions.
The Dodgers officially won’t reach their goal after being swept by the Milwaukee Brewers 4-0 in the National League Championship Series.
Skubal is now officially a free agent.
After the Brewers completed the sweep at Dodger Stadium on Thursday night, Skubal addressed his future.
Ex-Detroit Tigers LHP Tarik Skubal Makes Statement on Free Agency After Los Angeles Dodgers’ NLCS Loss to Milwaukee Brewers
Tarik Skubal on his impending free agency:
“I’m not going to comment on my future really at all. Today sucks, you know, and that’s kind of where my head’s at.”
It’ll be interesting to see how Skubal’s free agency goes. He should earn the largest free agent contract of any pitcher (except for Shohei Ohtani of course), but the looming lockout could affect his market.
Skubal may want to sign a contract before the lockout in case a salary cap is implemented and leads to him making less money. However, owners may not be willing to sign him until the lockout is over.
Looking at Tarik Skubal
LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA – OCTOBER 03: Tarik Skubal #29 of the Los Angeles Dodgers reacts to a defensive play by Tommy Edman #25 (not pictured) during the fourth inning in game one of the National League Division Series against the Atlanta Braves at Dodger Stadium on October 03, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Luke Hales/Getty Images)
The Tigers traded Skubal, the back-to-back AL Cy Young Award winner, to the Dodgers for outfielder Zyhir Hope, right-hander River Ryan and right-hander Brady Smith.
During the regular season, Skubal went 12-7 with a 2.72 ERA and 186 strikeouts over 158 2/3 innings.
LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA – OCTOBER 03: Tarik Skubal #29 of the Los Angeles Dodgers warms up prior to game one of the National League Division Series against the Atlanta Braves at Dodger Stadium on October 03, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Ryan Sirius Sun/Getty Images)
He missed over two months of the season with Detroit due to loose bodies in his left elbow that required surgery.
In this year’s postseason, Skubal posted a 2.45 ERA with 14 strikeouts in 11 innings across two starts.
LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA – SEPTEMBER 19: Tarik Skubal #29 of the Los Angeles Dodgers reacts to a walk to Osleivis Basabe #39 of the San Francisco Giants during the second inning at Dodger Stadium on September 19, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Harry How/Getty Images)
The Tigers selected Skubal in the ninth round (No. 255 overall) of the 2018 MLB Draft out of Seattle.
Skubal made his MLB debut in 2020.
LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA – AUGUST 22: Tarik Skubal #29 of the Los Angeles Dodgers pitches against the Pittsburgh Pirates during the third inning at Dodger Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Luke Hales/Getty Images)
The left-hander posted a 3.04 ERA with 1,005 strikeouts in 863 1/3 innings across seven seasons with the Tigers.
Skubal led the American League in ERA in 2024 and 2025, earning him back-to-back Cy Young awards.

item.title: [Motor City Bengals] Tarik Skubal's dance around free agency is posturing Tigers fans know all too well
item.dc:creator: Katrina Stebbins
item.description: On Thursday night, the mighty Dodgers were swept out of the NLCS by the scrappy Brewers, much to the delight of every baseball fan with even an ounce of enmity for the two-time champions (the majority of baseball fans, at this point). Tigers fans get to take a particular joy in the loss. Tarik Skubal might not have been able to choose where he was traded, but it was made far more painful for the fact that it was to the Dodgers. He maintained the party line when, after the deal was done, he said,
item.content:encoded:
On Thursday night, the mighty Dodgers were swept out of the NLCS by the scrappy Brewers, much to the delight of every baseball fan with even an ounce of enmity for the two-time champions (the majority of baseball fans, at this point).
Tigers fans get to take a particular joy in the loss. Tarik Skubal might not have been able to choose where he was traded, but it was made far more painful for the fact that it was to the Dodgers. He maintained the party line when, after the deal was done, he said, "Anyone could've traded for me."
Skubal made one start in the NLCS and disappointed, going just five innings with two earned runs. LA looked overpowered by Milwaukee at every possible turn. Even in Game 4, the Dodgers got out to a 4-0 lead in the second inning ... but they didn't score again. The Brewers slowly chipped away at the lead before overcoming it in the sixth inning and eventually winning 6-4.
Unsurprisingly, Skubal was asked about his impending free agency as the Dodgers were licking their wounds in the clubhouse. He said, "I'm not going to comment on my future really at all. Today sucks, you know, and that's kind of where my head's at."
Yeah, Tigers fans know that dance all too well.
Tarik Skubal refuses to take questions about his free agency after Dodgers are swept in NLCS
Much of the frustration with Skubal in his last year with the Tigers revolved around his cageyness around his future with the team and his free agency. That's his prerogative as a free agent, and one who will probably make a record-breaking amount of money when he signs, but it was his apparent unwillingness to even come to the table with the Tigers over an extension that really rankled fans.
There was nuance there, like anything else, and the Tigers deserve their fair share of the blame, but Tigers fans know that Skubal isn't going to reveal anything that might hurt his ability to negotiate.
The Dodgers are still widely thought of as the favorites to sign him, for obvious reasons. However, the Mets are preparing to creep in, and might be desperate enough to pay him well beyond even the highly-cited $400 million estimation.
Skubal isn't going to make it easy on them, which is another reason why we're almost certainly not going to see the Tigers involved in the bidding. Good luck, Dodgers (and Mets) fans. You're in for a bumpy ride.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] The Long-Awaited Tarik Skubal Sweepstakes Is Here and Could Get Pricey

item.content:encoded:
The 2026 season is over for the Los Angeles Dodgers.
Los Angeles entered the 2026 season hoping for a historic third-straight World Series title, but those dreams were crushed by the National League Central champion Milwaukee Brewers. On paper, the Dodgers have the most star-studded roster in the league and Milwaukee looks more like the little engine that could. And it certainly did. The Brewers swept the Dodgers and now they have a longer-than-expected offseason ahead. Plus, the Dodgers employ the player who will be the biggest question mark in baseball in free agency: Tarik Skubal.
The Skubal sweepstakes is here and over the next few months, the two-time Cy Young Award winner will dominate free agency chatter because there is a real chance that he becomes the highest-paid pitcher in MLB history.
Over the last few years, there has tended to be at least one mega star heading to the open market. We've seen Shohei Ohtani, Juan Soto and Kyle Tucker all land massive deals over the last few years, for example. This winter, all eyes will be on Skubal. After Los Angeles was knocked out on Thursday, Skubal was asked about free agency, but he wasn't ready to talk about it, as shared by Sonja Chen of MLB.com.
"I'm not going to comment on my future really at all. Today sucks, you know, and that's kind of where my head's at," Skubal said.
Breaking Down Tarik Skubal's Market
While Skubal wasn't ready to discuss the market yet, the baseball world will certainly be. Skubal is about to cash in this winter and it will be among the biggest stories of the year, outside of the ongoing collective bargaining agreement negotiations and the upcoming winner of the World Series. Skubal's market could be that big. Right now, Spotrac has his market value projected to be just over $276 million across seven years. That would be an annual value of over $39 million per year. Right now, the record for the largest deal given to a pitcher by total value was Yoshinobu Yamamoto's $325 million over 12 years from the Los Angeles Dodgers. Zack Wheeler of the Philadelphia Phillies has the highest annual value of starters right now at $42 million (three-year, $126 million).
Back in September, ESPN's Jeff Passan wrote in a column that if a salary cap isn't added this winter, Skubal has a shot at doubling the $245 million deal Stephen Strasburg got from the Washington Nationals. That would be a truly absurd contract, especially because of the fact that Skubal will be 30 years old in just a few weeks. Plus, let's not forget that he had elbow surgery this season. He was great on the hill afterward, but you've always got to think about elbows when it comes to pitchers, especially if they have past question marks there.
When free agency opens up, Skubal is going to get paid very well. But how much? And by who? Also will the potential lockout speed the process up?
This winter, Skubal is the straw that will stir the drink in free agency. His market is going to be so large that it will likely impact other hurlers — and potentially the top free agents in general. We saw similar situations with other top free agents, like Soto. His market pretty much hung up free agency as he decided his next move. Skubal's sweepstakes has the potential to do the same. When all is said and done, Skubal is going to land some mega, nine-figure deal. There's a real chance he could break Yamamoto's record for the largest pitcher contract ever. With the Dodgers' season now over, the sweepstakes officially begins.
Patrick McAvoy's experiences include local and national sports coverage at the New England Sports Network with a focus on baseball and basketball. Outside of journalism, Patrick also received an MBA at Brandeis University. For all business/marketing inquiries regarding Fastball On SI, please reach out to Scott Neville: scott@moreviewsmedia.com

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] 5 Tarik Skubal landing spots (Mets?) as free agency begins for Dodgers ace
item.dc:creator: Charles Curtis; For The Win

The two-time Cy Young winner was dealt to the Dodgers mid-season and finished with a 2.36 ERA in 10 regular-season games, and with a labor dispute looming, things could get complicated even if he's the biggest name by far on the market. Still, it's worth asking: Where will the soon-to-be 30-year-old ace
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are officially out of the 2026 MLB playoffs after an NLCS sweep at the hands of the Milwaukee Brewers, and that means the clock has started on Tarik Skubal's free agency.
The two-time Cy Young winner was dealt to the Dodgers mid-season and finished with a 2.36 ERA in 10 regular-season games, and with a labor dispute looming, things could get complicated even if he's the biggest name by far on the market. Still, it's worth asking: Where will the soon-to-be 30-year-old ace sign?
Let's dive in with five teams who could be possible landing spots as the bidding begins, in no particular order:
Los Angeles Dodgers
The obvious answer. He re-signs in L.A. for a ton of money -- maybe some of it deferred -- and the Dodgers keep one of the best pitchers in baseball. It wouldn't be that surprising given that they traded for him in the first place.
Now we get into the list of teams that can afford a player like Skubal (but hey, if there's a salary cap! We won't assume anything about that just yet). The Mets and their deep-pocketed owner would be happy to make a splash and secure a front-line starter, something New York needs going into next season.
Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole, Carlos Rodon... and Skubal? That would be downright nasty. There might be questions about the Yankees' lineup heading into this offseason, but a signing like that will silence some of the overall questions.
They could use an ace and we've seen Toronto be in the mix for big-name free agents before. This wouldn't be too crazy of a landing spot for Skubal.
Garrett Crochet is awesome, but beyond that, the Red Sox could use some front-line starter help. Does the franchise take out the checkbook here?
This article originally appeared on For The Win: 5 Tarik Skubal landing spots (Mets?) as free agency begins for Dodgers ace

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers dynasty is over, or has at least hit a major bump in the road. Thursday's Game 4 loss to the Milwaukee Brewers completed the four-game sweep and sent the two-time defending World Series champions home for the winter. Los Angeles' season is over, as is its stretch of eight consecutive postseason series wins dating back to 2024.
There is no getting around it: The Dodgers looked old in the NLCS. They are old too. Weighed by playing time, they had baseball's oldest collection of position players this season. Will Smith is 31. Shohei Ohtani is 32. Mookie Betts and Teoscar Hernández are 34. Freddie Freeman is 37. The team's core hitters are getting long in the tooth. It was obvious in the NLCS.
That said, the Dodgers remain extremely talented and have the resources (money and tradeable prospects) to improve their roster in the offseason, and again contend in 2027. As bad as they looked in the NLCS, there is no reason to think the Dodgers won't be among baseball's best teams next year -- and on the short list of legitimate World Series contenders.
Here now are three questions facing the Dodgers following their unceremonious NLCS sweep.
1. What is Shohei Ohtani's future?
The two-way star was hindered by health for a large chunk of 2026
In fact, let's talk about his future both short- and long-term. Ohtani was clearly diminished late in the regular season and into the postseason. He played through knee and biceps injuries and simply did not look like himself at the plate. His swing was all arms and there was little hard contact. Before his second-inning home run in Game 4 on Thursday, Ohtani hadn't gone deep since Aug. 18. His power vanished.
Here is Ohtani's expected slugging percentage, which is based on contact quality (exit velocity, launch angle, etc.), throughout this season. It slipped significantly late in the year:
Ohtani did not pitch after July 3 and had a start-and-stop in late August. He rehabbed his injuries, threw bullpen sessions and live batting practice, then had to shut it down before getting back on a mound in a game. Ohtani was playing like his usual MVP self until his injuries popped up in the second half. Once that happened, his season began to circle the drain.
The Dodgers now face two questions with Ohtani. One, does he need offseason surgery on the knee and/or biceps? And if he does need surgery, will the recovery cut into his 2027? Keep in mind that it is a near certainty there will be a lockout this offseason once the CBA expires on Dec. 1, and teams will be banned from communicating with their players. Ohtani would have to rehab on his own, without the team's input.
"It's hard to tell" if he'll require surgery, Ohtani said through an interpreter after Thursday's loss. He does, however, plan to pitch next season, he said.
Offseason surgery is the short-term question. Long-term, regardless of what he said in the shadow of the NLCS sweep, are Ohtani's days as a pitcher numbered? This has been a question since Day 1 of Ohtani's MLB career. His ability to be and remain a two-way player has long been doubted, but he has kept doing it, even if there have been some speed bumps along the way. Ohtani has made a career of doing what people said he couldn't.
The man is 32 now, though. He'll turn 33 next summer and the physical ailments (the knee, the biceps, two UCL surgeries, etc.) are beginning to add up. At some point, Ohtani won't be able to continue as a two-way player, and with each passing season, that point draws closer. Are we there now? Is this it? Is this the end of Ohtani's time as a pitcher? It could be, sure.
My guess is that Ohtani will continue to pitch next season and the Dodgers will happily let him because there is so much value to be gained even if he throws only 75 innings a year. You can't be as good as Ohtani without being stubborn. He's been stubborn in that he insists on playing both ways, and he has continued to do it well. I don't see him dropping it this winter.
It should surprise no one if Ohtani comes out next year, hits 40 home runs, makes 15 ace-caliber starts and wins his fifth MVP unanimously. Do not forget that he was playing at that level as recently as July. The recovery times for the knee and biceps injuries are an offseason question, for sure, and the bottom line is the "will he continue to pitch?" questions will always exist.
2. Will they move on from some longtime stalwarts?
Could the Dodgers say goodbye to Teoscar Hernández or some other familiar names?
The Dodgers are locked into so much of their core: Betts, Freeman, Ohtani, Smith, Kyle Tucker, etc. They aren't going anywhere. That said, there are a few members of the supporting cast, players who have been around for all three recent World Series wins, who might have to be shown the door this offseason for the sake of diversifying the lineup and getting younger and more athletic.
Finding a taker for the final season of Teoscar Hernández's contract and then plugging the precocious Josue De Paula into left field next season is a worthwhile move. It's difficult because Hernández is popular in the clubhouse, but, on the field, De Paula figures to give the Dodgers a better chance to win ballgames moving forward. (De Paula is a poor defender, but so is Hernández.)
The Enrique Hernández era has run its course. He hasn't been even an average regular-season player since 2022, and, for all his postseason heroics, he's barely scraping a .600 OPS in the last two Octobers. Tommy Edman is a better version of the same player. There's no need to carry both on the roster, plus Edman's injuries suggest a smaller role is needed. Less could be more.
Max Muncy stayed healthy this season, hit 29 homers and posted 4.1 WAR, and is owed an affordable $10 million in 2027. Plus, it's a bad offseason to need an infielder. The free-agent market is very thin and you're not likely to find better than Muncy on the trade market. Still, he is 36. Keeping Muncy is justifiable, but it also makes sense to explore alternatives. It never hurts to look.
Blake Treinen has not been healthy and effective at the same time in two years. Alex Vesia's fastball sat 91-92 mph over these last few weeks. Both are free agents and the Dodgers have so many young hard-throwers in Triple-A that I think it's worth turning the page and injecting some younger arms into the bullpen. Evan Phillips may be in this camp, too.
Then again, who am I to doubt the Dodgers and their process? Disappointing NLCS aside, they have been baseball's most successful team of the 2020s, and if they want to remain in the Hernández and Muncy and Treinen business, I won't say they're wrong. It does appear that things are getting a bit stale, though. Incorporating youth would be sensible, and it isn't difficult to find ways to do it.
3. Will they retain Tarik Skubal?
It will cost a lot to keep the trade deadline addition atop the rotation
There's no sense in asking if the Dodgers can retain Tarik Skubal. Of course they can. They are baseball's biggest spenders and he is a Scott Boras client. Typically, all you need to do to get a Boras client is make the biggest offer, which the Dodgers can do. Maybe there's a salary cap that changes the equation. Based on what we know right now, yes, the Dodgers can, of course, re-sign Skubal.
Will they is a different matter. Tyler Glasnow, Blake Snell, and Yoshinobu Yamamoto will return next season. Ohtani could be back on the mound as well, as he indicated is the plan. Emmet Sheehan and Justin Wrobleski both pitched well for long stretches this year and are among the very best No. 5 starter options in the game. Gavin Stone, the team's 2024 innings leader, should return from shoulder surgery as well.
There is never a bad time to sign a pitcher like Skubal, and the Dodgers, with their World Series window still open, are well-positioned to bring him back. They have the money, they can easily clear rotation space, and all indications are that Skubal enjoyed his time with the team after coming over the trade deadline. This feels like a match made in free-agent heaven.
Now it's just a matter of whether the Dodgers can get it done. Perhaps a salary cap or increased competitive balance tax penalties limit their spending; maybe they opt to spread their money around to multiple players; maybe another team just won't be denied. The Dodgers don't absolutely need Skubal. Re-signing him would up their odds of returning to the World Series, though, and help ensure their dynasty didn't end on Thursday night.
For his part, Skubal declined to comment on his impending decision after Game 4.
"I'm not going to comment on my future really at all," Skubal said, via MLB.com. "Today sucks, you know, and that's kind of where my head's at."

item.title: [fansided.com] These 5 Dodgers won't be back next year after three-peat bid crashes and burns
item.dc:creator: Zachary Rotman
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers appeared poised to three-peat as World Series champions. item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers appeared poised to three-peat as World Series champions. They loaded up after winning their second straight title, signing Kyle Tucker and Edwin Diaz in free agency and trading for Tarik Skubal at the trade deadline. All they had to do was get through a Milwaukee Brewers team they swept in last year's NLCS in order to appear in a World Series against either Tampa Bay or Cleveland, both of whom L.A. would be favored to take care of.
Instead, the Dodgers' incredible run was stymied by Milwaukee in an NLCS that can only be classified as embarrassing for L.A. The Dodgers could not get anything going offensively, and their vaunted rotation underwhelmed. Now, with their three-peat bid having been a failure, an important offseason is ahead. Will Tarik Skubal be back? That shouldn't be ruled out. These other players, though, almost certainly won't be back with the Dodgers seeking revenge in 2027 (if there even is a 2027 season).
INF Miguel Rojas
Why not start out with an easy one? Miguel Rojas has made it clear that he plans on retiring after the 2026 campaign. He can always change his mind, and he told Maddie Lee of the Los Angeles Times that he wouldn't play for another team, but with Rojas now 37 years old and with a pair of World Series wins on his resume, what more does he have to play for?
Rojas retiring would be a tough blow for the Dodgers, given the fact that he's still a solid bench piece, is an important clubhouse presence, and recorded one of the biggest and unlikeliest hits in MLB history when he tied Game 7 of the 2025 World Series with a home run, but it's hard to imagine Rojas sticking around for another year.
RHP Blake Treinen
Once upon a time, Blake Treinen was one of the best relievers in the sport. He saved 38 games for the Athletics in 2018, and had a pair of sub-2.00 ERA seasons for the Dodgers in 2021 and 2024. Unfortunately, Treinen has a 4.47 ERA in 68 appearances since the start of the 2025 campaign, and injuries have limited him to fewer than 40 outings in each of those years.
Treinen missed nearly three months of the 2026 campaign with elbow inflammation, didn't pitch all that great upon his return, and was placed on the IL with shoulder inflammation at the end of the regular season. Injuries have been a common theme for Treinen over the course of his career, and while he had always been good enough to keep around despite his missed time, now, at 38 years old, he isn't what he once was. It's hard to envision the Dodgers being eager to bring him back.
LHP Kris Bubic
The Dodgers bolstered their pitching depth by acquiring Kris Bubic at the trade deadline from the Kansas City Royals. Sure, Bubic was hurt at the time, which made the move a bit risky, but L.A. made this move with the postseason in mind. Well, while Bubic came through with five scoreless appearances in the regular season, he allowed a run in each of his postseason appearances, taking a loss in the NLDS against the Braves and blowing a rare lead the Dodgers had in Game 2 of the NLCS against the Brewers.
These rough outings aren't reason enough to not want to bring Bubic back, but odds are, the southpaw is going to want to start (he was rock-solid in that role with the Royals), and I'm not sold that the Dodgers will be eager to guarantee him a rotation spot, with Shohei Ohtani, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell, Tyler Glasnow locked in if healthy, and guys like Justin Wrobleski, Roki Sasaki and Emmet Sheehan still in the organization. Odds are, Bubic will earn a solidified rotation spot elsewhere.
LHP Eric Lauer
The Dodgers dealt with a slew of pitching injuries, and brought Eric Lauer in to give them needed depth. To his credit, Lauer pitched quite well in his 13 appearances (11 starts) for the Dodgers. In fact, He allowed three earned runs or fewer in nine of his 11 starts and allowed just one run in eight innings in two appearances as a bulk reliever. If it weren't for a couple of especially brutal starts, Lauer's numbers in L.A. would've wound up looking much better than they did.
With that being said, Lauer ended the year on the IL with left elbow inflammation and, as is the case with Bubic, is probably looking for more of a solidified role than the Dodgers would be willing to give him. He'd be a solid option to bring back in a swingman role, but it's likely that the 31-year-old will end up elsewhere.
OF Teoscar Hernandez
Here's the big one. Teoscar Hernandez is the only player on this list under contract for 2027, and he's been a staple in L.A. since the 2024 campaign. There're a couple of reasons why it makes sense to move him, though. First, he's simply not worth the $17 million he's owed in 2027 after the year he just had. He still mashes left-handed pitching, but he had a subpar .695 OPS against righties in the regular season and is a very poor defensive outfielder. It's hard to justify playing him regularly on a team trying to contend.
Second, and perhaps most importantly, the Dodgers need to find a spot for top prospect Josue De Paula to play regularly. The ideal spot for De Paula, an outstanding hitter whose defense leaves much to be desired, would be DH, but that's Shohei Ohtani's spot for the foreseeable future. Kyle Tucker is locked into right field given his absurd contract, and De Paula can't play center field (nor should the Dodgers be eager to move off of Andy Pages). That leaves left field, Hernandez's spot, as the position where De Paula seems likeliest to slot in.
The Dodgers can keep Hernandez around as a platoon partner for De Paula, but a trade could make sense. Hernandez was in rumors last offseason, and I wouldn't be surprised to see those resurface this winter.

item.title: [CBS Sports] What Tarik Skubal said about his pending free agency after Dodgers' playoff elimination
item.dc:creator: Matt Snyder
item.description: Ace left-hander Tarik Skubal watched his Dodgers get eliminated in the NLCS from the dugout in Game 4 on Thursday night. item.content:encoded:
Ace left-hander Tarik Skubal watched his Dodgers get eliminated in the NLCS from the dugout in Game 4 on Thursday night. Now, Skubal's next stop is free agency this coming offseason. He will be the top free agent on the market and command an absurd amount of money before signing on the dotted line.
Unsurprisingly, Skubal didn't have much to say on the matter after Game 4.
"I'm not going to comment on my future really at all," he said, via MLB.com. "Today sucks, you know, and that's kind of where my head's at."
Skubal heads to free agency having made the playoffs for three straight years and posted a 2.13 ERA in eight playoff starts, but his teams have been unable to make the World Series. In fact, the trip to the NLCS this year with the Dodgers was the deepest he's ever been in the playoffs. The Tigers made the ALDS in both 2024 and 2025 before being eliminated.
The 29-year-old Skubal was the American League Cy Young winner in both 2024 and 2025. This season, he suffered an injury to his pitching elbow that required surgery, a new procedure called NanoScope surgery. He healed remarkably quickly, only missing starts between April 29 and June 13.
Nine starts later and the Tigers -- despite only being 2 ½ games out of a playoff spot -- decided to get in front of missing the postseason and losing Skubal to free agency. They traded him to the Dodgers at the deadline for a package that included top prospect Zyhir Hope.
Between the two teams this season, Skubal made 26 starts and went 12-7 with a 2.72 ERA (155 ERA+), 0.96 WHIP and 186 strikeouts in 158 ⅔ innings. His 4.6 WAR was down from 6.7 and 6.4, respectively, in the previous two seasons, but he made five fewer starts.
Normally, a pitcher like Skubal hitting free agency would mean bidding into the mid-nine-figure range, but there's uncertainty this time around with the CBA expiring and the ownership side driving hard toward a salary cap. It's possible that Skubal's contract needs to wait until after a deal is made between the two sides and teams know what they have to work with in their finances. Conversely, a team could be incredibly aggressive in trying to get his deal grandfathered under the previous CBA. Time will tell.
For now, Skubal and the rest of the Dodgers head home for the winter.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers won’t three-peat as World Series Champions.
The Milwaukee Brewers completed a 4-0 sweep of the Dodgers in the National League Championship Series with a 6-4 win at Dodger Stadium on Thursday.
The Brewers will play the winner of the American League Championship Series between the Cleveland Guardians and Tampa Bay Rays in the Fall Classic.
Two-time Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal is now a free agent. After Thursday’s game, Skubal was asked about entering the free agent market.
Tarik Skubal Makes Statement on Free Agency After Los Angeles Dodgers’ NLCS Loss to Milwaukee Brewers
LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA – OCTOBER 04: Tarik Skubal #29 of the Los Angeles Dodgers warms up before the game against the Atlanta Braves in game two of the National League Division Series at Dodger Stadium on October 04, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Katelyn Mulcahy/Getty Images)
Tarik Skubal on his impending free agency:
“I’m not going to comment on my future really at all. Today sucks, you know, and that’s kind of where my head’s at.”
Looking at Tarik Skubal
LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA – OCTOBER 03: Tarik Skubal #29 of the Los Angeles Dodgers reacts to a defensive play by Tommy Edman #25 (not pictured) during the fourth inning in game one of the National League Division Series against the Atlanta Braves at Dodger Stadium on October 03, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Luke Hales/Getty Images)
The Detroit Tigers traded Skubal, the back-to-back AL Cy Young Award winner, to the Dodgers for outfielder Zyhir Hope, right-hander River Ryan and right-hander Brady Smith.
During the regular season, Skubal went 12-7 with a 2.72 ERA and 186 strikeouts over 158 2/3 innings.
LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA – OCTOBER 03: Tarik Skubal #29 of the Los Angeles Dodgers warms up prior to game one of the National League Division Series against the Atlanta Braves at Dodger Stadium on October 03, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Ryan Sirius Sun/Getty Images)
He missed over two months of the season with Detroit due to loose bodies in his left elbow that required surgery.
In this year’s postseason, Skubal posted a 2.45 ERA with 14 strikeouts in 11 innings across two starts.
LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA – SEPTEMBER 19: Tarik Skubal #29 of the Los Angeles Dodgers reacts to a walk to Osleivis Basabe #39 of the San Francisco Giants during the second inning at Dodger Stadium on September 19, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Harry How/Getty Images)
The Tigers selected Skubal in the ninth round (No. 255 overall) of the 2018 MLB Draft out of Seattle.
Skubal made his MLB debut in 2020.
LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA – AUGUST 22: Tarik Skubal #29 of the Los Angeles Dodgers pitches against the Pittsburgh Pirates during the third inning at Dodger Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Luke Hales/Getty Images)
The left-hander posted a 3.04 ERA with 1,005 strikeouts in 863 1/3 innings across seven seasons with the Tigers.
Skubal led the American League in ERA in 2024 and 2025, earning him back-to-back Cy Young awards.

item.title: [sgvtribune.com] Dodgers’ Shohei Ohtani returns to leadoff spot for must-win Game 4

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — Desperate times call for … unexpected measures.
Two days after admitting he had a conversation with Shohei Ohtani about taking him out of the lineup for Game 3 of the National League Championship Series and one day after dropping him to sixth in the order for that game, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts moved Ohtani back to the top of the lineup.
Ohtani was in the leadoff spot for Game 4 against the Milwaukee Brewers on Thursday. It was his first time batting leadoff this postseason.
“Just seeing the work the last couple days, I like where his head is at,” Roberts said. “I liked the at-bats yesterday, and I felt that trying to shake it up a little bit – obviously we haven’t performed the way that we’re capable of, so to kind of shake it up a little bit but something that’s of somewhat normalcy that our guys are used to.”
Ohtani is just 4 for 22 (.182) in the postseason, but that hardly stands out in the unproductive lineup. Through the first three games of the NLCS, the Dodgers were hitting .165 (15 for 91) as a team with just two extra-base hits and no home runs. Only Mookie Betts (3 for 12) had more than two hits.
“I think getting back to what we’ve done all year and how it’s been going recently as far as on the offense, I think it warranted just a little bit of a shakeup,” said Roberts, who also started Miguel Rojas and Kiké Hernandez against Brewers left-hander Shane Drohan.
PHILLY CONNECTION
Before re-signing Don Mattingly to a contract extension as manager, the Philadelphia Phillies reached out to two members of the Dodgers’ front office with Philly connections – Chase Utley and Raul Ibañez.
Neither would confirm the contact, but neither interviewed for the job. Both have teen-aged children and Utley acknowledged family takes priority over pursuing a managerial career at this point.
Ibañez, currently the Dodgers’ vice president of baseball development and special projects, has been approached about managing on other occasions but declined. Utley is a special assistant to Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman.
AWARDS SEASON
Despite his injuries and a prolonged slump, Ohtani is one of the National League finalists for the Hank Aaron Award given to the top offensive performer in MLB during the regular season. Ohtani finished the season with a .275 average, 30 home runs and an .889 OPS. Ohtani has won it the past three seasons (twice in the NL and once with the Angels in the American League).
The other finalists are CJ Abrams (Washington Nationals), Jake Bauers (Milwaukee Brewers), Pete Crow-Armstrong (Chicago Cubs), Elly De La Cruz and Sal Stewart (Cincinnati Reds), Matt Olson (Atlanta Braves), Kyle Schwarber (Philadelphia Phillies), Fernando Tatis Jr. (San Diego Padres) and Jordan Walker (St. Louis Cardinals).
Ohtani is also one of three finalists for the Players’ Choice Outstanding Player Award along with Crow-Armstrong and Schwarber.
Max Muncy and Andy Pages have been named finalists for Gold Glove awards at their positions. Muncy is a finalist at third base along with Alex Bregman (Cubs) and Javier Sanoja (Miami Marlins). Pages is a finalist in center field along with Crow-Armstrong and Michael Harris II (Braves).
The Gold Glove winners will be announced on ESPN on Nov. 1.
UP NEXT
NLCS Game 5 (if necessary): Brewers (RHP Jacob Misiorowski, 16-5, 1.80 ERA) at Dodgers (LHP Tarik Skubal, 12-7, 2.72 ERA), Friday, 6 p.m. FS1, 570 AM

item.title: [sgvtribune.com] Dodgers three-peat bid ends with NLCS sweep by Brewers
item.dc:creator: Bill Plunkett
item.description: LOS ANGELES — In the end, it was all too much – coming back from a 3-0 deficit, winning a third consecutive World Series championship. Shohei Ohtani came back to life after two months of ugly at-bats, unfamiliar criticism and questions about whether he even belonged in the Dodgers’ lineup. His three-run home run in the second inning on Thursday night gave the Dodgers a four-run lead – unheard of in this postseason of run suppression. That wasn’t enough to keep their season alive against a relent
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — In the end, it was all too much – coming back from a 3-0 deficit, winning a third consecutive World Series championship.
Shohei Ohtani came back to life after two months of ugly at-bats, unfamiliar criticism and questions about whether he even belonged in the Dodgers’ lineup. His three-run home run in the second inning on Thursday night gave the Dodgers a four-run lead – unheard of in this postseason of run suppression.
That wasn’t enough to keep their season alive against a relentless Milwaukee Brewers team that just kept coming, taking a 6-4 win in Game 4 on Thursday to complete a four-game sweep of the two-time defending champions and advance from the National League Championship Series to their first World Series in 44 years.
After falling behind on Garrett Mitchell’s home run off Tanner Scott in the sixth inning, the Dodgers put the tying run on third base with one out in the sixth, seventh and eighth innings but couldn’t move him another 90 feet. Their dreams of a three-peat were buried under another collection of failed at-bats with a runner in scoring position. They went 2 for 11 in those situations in Game 4 and 5 for 43 in the postseason.
“As a manager and anyone participating in the game, you always wonder … could we have done something different that could have changed the game?” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. “I think at the end of the day, we got beat. We got outplayed in all facets. Those guys played flawless defensively. They pitched better than we did. They hit better than we did. They slugged more than we did. You’ve got to sometimes just tip your cap.
“I personally told our guys that there’s no apologies, there’s no ‘Sorry’s. We gave it everything we had, and it wasn’t good enough. That’s part of life.”
The New York Yankees of 1998-2000 are still the most recent team to ‘three-peat’ as World Series champions. A National League franchise still hasn’t done it.
“It’s hard to win one. We won two,” Freddie Freeman said. “We went for three and we came up short on a third. Special stuff the past two years. We just came up short this year.”
After losing Game 3 on Wednesday night to become the 42nd team in MLB history to fall behind 3-0 in a best-of-seven series, the Dodgers said all the right things about becoming just the second to climb out of that hole and win the series.
“Four one-game winning streaks,” Dodgers utility player Kiké Hernandez said.
“We’ve won four in a row a number of times this year, ten times, I think,” Manager Dave Roberts said.
Ohtani gave them reason to believe.
With the Brewers rolling out a ‘bullpen game’ in Game 4, opener Shane Drohan was gone after a leadoff single by Kyle Tucker in the second inning. Former Dodger Dustin May replaced him and gave up another single to Teoscar Hernandez, struck out Max Muncy then gave up an RBI single to Andy Pages – the only Dodger who seemed able to hit with a runner in scoring position this postseason.
Kiké Hernandez flew out, bringing Ohtani to the plate with two outs. He struck out against Drohan in the first inning but had finished Game 3 with a 113.5 mph exit velocity on an eighth-inning single – the kind of hard contact missing from Ohtani since mid-August and one of the signs that convinced Roberts to move him back to the leadoff spot for Game 4.
May threw Ohtani a 1-and-1 cutter in at his knees and Ohtani crushed it. It left his bat at 113.1 mph and traveled 428 feet into the right field pavilion. The emotion that burst out of Ohtani was just as explosive. As the crowd roared, he bounced down the first-base line, screaming and gesturing at his teammates in the dugout.
It looked like things were finally turning the Dodgers’ way in this series.
“It’s hard to not say yeah to that,” Muncy said. “He gets that moment, it’s like that’s the swing we’ve been waiting for. We got a nice lead, we got Glas on the mound, we’re confident behind him and they just kept stringing together one good at-bat after another after another after another. They were just kind of relentless.”
The Dodgers’ first home run in the NLCS ended the longest home-run drought of Ohtani’s career at 25 games and 116 plate appearances.
The only thing that seemed longer was how long the Dodgers were going to have to work to make that four-run second inning stand up.
It began disappearing in the fourth inning.
Starter Tyler Glasnow retired the first 10 Brewers in order and struck out six of the first eight. He didn’t have another strikeout. It was nothing but contact from the Brewers after that.
A walk and back-to-back ground-rule doubles – the second by Jake Bauers – cut the Dodgers’ lead in half. An inning later, Glasnow walked the No. 8 hitter, Sal Frelick, who stole second and scored on a single by the No. 9 hitter David Hamilton.
Glasnow was replaced by Evan Phillips who walked three in a row (one intentionally after Hamilton stole second) to force in the tying run.
The four aces the Dodgers thought would give them the upper hand in this postseason did not. Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Glasnow combined for a 6.50 ERA in the series against the Brewers. Only Skubal allowed fewer than three runs in his start.
Tanner Scott came on for the sixth inning. He didn’t give up a home run to a left-handed batter all season. The Brewers’ first batter in the sixth, left-handed Garrett Mitchell, has just two home runs off left-handed pitchers in his 286 career regular-season games.
Scott left a full-count fastball over the heart of the plate and Mitchell, a former UCLA and Orange Lutheran standout, sent it over the center field wall for his second home run off a left-handed pitcher in three at-bats (Blake Snell in Game 3).
The Brewers’ bullpen took over from there. The Dodgers got Kyle Tucker to third base after his one-out double in the sixth, Pages to third after his leadoff double in the seventh and Will Smith to third when Brewers right fielder Frelick fumbled his double in the right field corner.
The six at-bats with a chance to push across the tying run ended in three strikeouts, two ground outs and a shallow pop up to center field.
Hamilton made it a two-run lead with a solo home run in the top of the ninth. It was just the fifth hit of the game for the Brewers.
More to come on this story.

item.title: [mlb.com] Brewers end Dodgers' three-peat bid with an NLCS sweep of their own
item.dc:creator: AJ Cassavell
item.description: LOS ANGELES -- For 363 days, the Brewers dreamed of a different ending. On Thursday night, they wrote it. The script? Familiar enough. A National League Championship Series sweep culminating at Dodger Stadium. Only this time, it was the Brewers who poured from the first-base dugout, celebrating an NL pennant decades in the making -- and celebrating in the very ballpark where their previous season had come to such an unceremonious end. The two-time defending champion Dodgers have been dethroned.
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES -- For 363 days, the Brewers dreamed of a different ending. On Thursday night, they wrote it.
The script? Familiar enough. A National League Championship Series sweep culminating at Dodger Stadium. Only this time, it was the Brewers who poured from the first-base dugout, celebrating an NL pennant decades in the making -- and celebrating in the very ballpark where their previous season had come to such an unceremonious end.
The two-time defending champion Dodgers have been dethroned. For the first time in 44 years, the Brewers are heading to the World Series. They beat Los Angeles, 6-4, in Game 4 on Thursday night. Next week, Milwaukee will host the Fall Classic for the first time since 1982.
And could this ending have been any more fitting?
Three times in the last decade, the Brewers had been expelled from the postseason by Los Angeles. A year ago, they were swept away with relative ease, as the Dodgers set a course for their second consecutive World Series title. It went unspoken, but all summer, the Brewers seemed to know: If they were going to get where they wanted to go, this was the team they needed to beat.
Thursday’s clincher did not come easy. Why should it? These Brewers don’t do easy. They fell behind 4-0 in the second inning. Dodger Stadium shook when Shohei Ohtani’s titanic three-run blast landed deep in the right-field pavilion.
But the Brewers did what these Brewers do. They answered. Two runs in the fourth. Two more in the fifth. Garrett Mitchell’s go-ahead home run in the sixth, and David Hamilton’s insurance blast in the ninth. Shortly thereafter, the Brewers were celebrating a first in MLB history: They became the first team to sweep the very same team that had eliminated them via sweep in the previous postseason.
Across four games, every punch the Dodgers threw was returned with a Milwaukee counterpunch. Facing elimination on Thursday, Los Angeles moved Ohtani back into the leadoff spot. He’s the best player on the planet, when healthy, and if the Dodgers were going to go down … why go down with anyone else at the top of their lineup?
That meant it was Ohtani who strode to the plate against Brewers right-handed reliever Dustin May with two on and two out in the second. May threw a 1-1 cutter. It hung. Ohtani unleashed that ferocious left-handed swing with a bit of an uppercut. (You know the one, even if it had been a while since you last saw it.) The ball carried to the very back of the right-field pavilion, Ohtani’s first home run since Aug. 18.
Dodger Stadium erupted. The two-time defending champs had life. They led 4-0 in the second inning. They had Tarik Skubal lined up for Game 5. And Yoshinobu Yamamoto for Game 6. And Blake Snell for Game 7. Maybe, just maybe …
The Brewers had other ideas. William Contreras and Jake Bauers hit back-to-back doubles in the fourth, cutting the Dodgers’ lead to 4-2. An inning later, Sal Frelick walked and stole a base, then scored on Hamilton’s RBI single. Tyler Glasnow’s night was done after 4 1/3 innings. A few batters later, Bauers plated the tying run with a bases-loaded walk.
Mitchell led off the sixth by pulverizing a Tanner Scott fastball, and the Brewers had the lead. They held onto it for dear life. Aaron Ashby stranded the tying run in scoring position in the seventh. Then again in the eighth.
He just kept going. Ashby got Kiké Hernández to line out to Jackson Chourio in left field to end it, and with that, the Brewers had their first National League pennant. (When they last reached the Fall Classic in 1982, they did so in the American League.) In the coming weeks, they’ll get a chance for another first: their first World Series title. Either the Rays or Guardians will stand in their way.
But first, a party 44 years in the making.

item.title: [FanSided] Tarik Skubal is more likely to leave the Dodgers after NLCS sweep
item.dc:creator: Zachary Rotman
item.description: It felt like the Los Angeles Dodgers were all but guaranteed another World Series title when they acquired Tarik Skubal at the trade deadline. Not only did they prevent Skubal from joining a contender like the Brewers, but they added Skubal to a rotation that already included Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow. Well, the Dodgers were swept in the NLCS by the same Brewers team that they swept just a year ago in the same round, and now, have to look ahead to the offseason. Most of t
item.content:encoded:
It felt like the Los Angeles Dodgers were all but guaranteed another World Series title when they acquired Tarik Skubal at the trade deadline. Not only did they prevent Skubal from joining a contender like the Brewers, but they added Skubal to a rotation that already included Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow. Well, the Dodgers were swept in the NLCS by the same Brewers team that they swept just a year ago in the same round, and now, have to look ahead to the offseason.
Most of their core is locked up (whether that's a good thing or not can be debated), but the one key exception is Skubal, who is slated to hit free agency and search for a record-setting contract. There's a pretty good chance that Skubal is going to surpass Yamamoto's 12-year, $325 million deal - the richest for a pitcher in MLB history (excluding Shohei Ohtani, for obvious reasons). Will the Dodgers be the team that pays him, though? It's always possible, but I lean no. Here're a couple of reasons why.
Are we sure the Dodgers will be the high bidder for Tarik Skubal?
This comes down to the money. Tarik Skubal did not hire Scott Boras to represent him to take a hometown discount anywhere. If he did, he'd likely have stayed with the Detroit Tigers. Sure, the Dodgers being perennial contenders in Southern California likely gives them a tiebreaker if all else is equal, but are we sure the Dodgers will be eager to go to insane lengths to keep him around?
Even without Skubal, the Dodgers have a rotation featuring options like Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Shohei Ohtani, Blake Snell, Tyler Glasnow, Emmet Sheehan, Justin Wrobleski, and Roki Sasaki. That is already a group that's as good as any, and as deep as any, without them even making a single addition. Sure, they'd like to have Skubal back, but at what cost?
There will be desperate suitors out there. The New York Mets could use an ace and have Steve Cohen's money to work with, coming off a dismal year. The Toronto Blue Jays are another big-market team in need of pitching with the deep pockets to spend on anybody. The Chicago Cubs might be persuaded to spend on pitching, especially with the Brewers now World Series-bound. Maybe a team like the Philadelphia Phillies will be willing to spend on a super-rotation.
The Dodgers can outbid any of these teams, but will they have the desire to, especially given Mark Walter's recent financial troubles? I'm not sure, especially when considering what they've already invested in their roster.
Dodgers have already invested so much money into their roster
Even the Dodgers have limits. Whether there's a salary cap or not, the Dodgers will only do so much. Given the money they've tied up, are they really willing to spend $300 million or $400 million on Skubal?
| Player | Contract | Age | Final Contract Year |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shohei Ohtani | 10 years, $700 million (with $680 million deferred) | 32 | 2033 |
| Mookie Betts | 12 years, $365 million | 34 | 2032 |
| Yoshinobu Yamamoto | 12 years, $325 million | 28 | 2035 (opt-outs after '30, '32) |
| Kyle Tucker | 4 years, $240 million | 29 | 2029 (opt-outs after '27, '28) |
| Blake Snell | 5 years, $182 million | 33 | 2030 (club option) |
| Freddie Freeman | 6 years, $162 million | 37 | 2027 |
| Will Smith | 10 years, $140 million | 31 | 2033 |
| Tyler Glasnow | 5 years, $136 million | 33 | 2028 (club option) |
| Tommy Edman | 5 years, $74 million | 31 | 2030 (club option) |
| Tanner Scott | 4 years, $72 million | 32 | 2028 |
| Edwin Diaz | 3 years, $69 million | 32 | 2029 |
| Teoscar Hernandez | 3 years, $66 million | 34 | 2028 (club option) |
The 2027 season hasn't even begun, yet the Dodgers already have a $393 million luxury tax payroll per Spotrac, the largest in the sport by nearly $50 million. Are they really going to be open to add more than $30 million annually to that, knowing they have other needs to address? I mean, their bullpen was shaky much of the year, and their lineup, clearly, has holes.
Again, even the Dodgers have limits. There's only a certain amount of money they'll be willing to invest. Adding another massive contract to this list feels like a lot to ask for, even for the Dodgers.
The last thing the Dodgers need is another bad contract on their hands
The Dodgers got the most out of the massive contracts they dolled out. Guys like Mookie Betts, Freddie Freeman, Will Smith and Teoscar Hernandez played a major role in their back-to-back World Series wins. It's also worth noting that this foursome had the worst years of their careers and that they're all on the wrong side of 30. Father Time is undefeated, and while the beginnings of these massive contracts are always fun, the later years almost never are.
It's clear that guys like Betts and Freeman are well beyond their respective primes at this point, and while Freeman's contract is expiring after 2027, Betts is locked in for another six years. Smith is under contract for another seven years. Blake Snell can't stay healthy and he's locked in for at least three more years. Based on how he played this year, the Dodgers might be stuck handing Kyle Tucker $60 million annually for the next three years. Ohtani and Yamamoto are players who are still great when healthy, but eventually they'll age. There are bad contracts and the potential for bad contracts everywhere you turn on this Dodgers roster.
Again, giving these deals proved to be worthwhile, with the Dodgers earning back-to-back World Series wins, but there's a clear downside to handing out these insane long-term deals. Are the Dodgers willing to take on the risk with Skubal, who, by the way, had an elbow injury this season and has a pretty scary history of arm injuries?
The overarching takeaway from this series, beyond how good the Brewers looked, is how lethargic the Dodgers looked. They appeared completely overmatched at the plate, and that doesn't feel accidental given how old this roster is. Re-signing Skubal will be great for the short term but will almost certainly not age well. Given all the other bad deals on their roster, adding another one just doesn't feel like the smartest move, and Andrew Friedman is one of the smartest minds in the sport.

item.title: [Sportsnet.ca] Brewers sweep Dodgers in NLCS to book ticket to World Series
item.dc:creator: Ben Nicholson-Smith

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — With the score tied at four in the top of the sixth inning, Tanner Scott threw a fastball down the middle and Garrett Mitchell crushed it.
As the ball soared over the centre field wall at Dodger Stadium, reality set in for the two-time defending champions and their fans: their reign atop MLB might be ending. And a few innings later, when Aaron Ashby retired Kiké Hernandez for the final out of a 6-4 win in Game 4 of the NLCS, it was all over.
There were late chances to score Kyle Tucker from second and Will Smith from third, but in the end the Dodgers failed.
They’re a great team, but not the best team in baseball anymore, or even the best team in the National League. That honour goes to the Milwaukee Brewers, who secured the pennant with a sweep of the Dodgers thanks to Mitchell’s big swing, some tenacious rallies in the middle innings and impressive relief pitching.
The win overshadowed a dramatic home run from Shohei Ohtani and disappointed 49,104 fans still hoping for a third straight championship. Instead, it’s Milwaukee who will represent the National League in the World Series in a battle of small markets against either Cleveland or Tampa Bay.
All series, the Brewers outplayed the Dodgers. They hit more home runs, they played better defence and they pitched better. And really, that should come as no surprise. This team has reached the post-season eight of the last nine seasons, including each of the last four NL Central titles.
But still, the Dodgers are baseball’s preeminent team, so when Shohei Ohtani demolished a Dustin May cutter to give the Dodgers an early 4-0 lead, their path to victory seemed to open up again. As the ball soared into the right-field bleachers, Ohtani bounced backwards towards first base and yelled at his teammates in the third-base dugout. It may be the most emotion he’s ever shown on a big-league field.
Considering the context, Ohtani’s home run was all the more significant. Just two days ago, there was talk of benching him given his middling performance and knee and biceps injuries. Then came a stellar performance in Game 3 and his Game 4 home run, the first one he’s hit since August 18.
But aside from Ohtani’s big swing, the Dodgers simply didn’t have answers offensively. No one else homered in the NLCS. In fact, they had just five other extra-base hits this series — all doubles. A team known for its high-powered offence had produced backup-catcher type numbers when it counted most.
They needed to hit or see their season end, no in-between. And they didn’t hit, so their season ended.
The Brewers, on the other hand, managed just enough offence. David Hamilton added a late home run and breakout star Jake Bauers drove in three, including two with a pivotal double in the fourth inning. All series, they found answers against the Dodgers team that allowed the fewest runs in MLB this regular season.
Oddly enough, this will be the first time the Brewers represent the National League in the World Series. When they made it in 1982, they were still an American League team and lost to the Cardinals in seven games.
The Dodgers were seeking the first MLB three-peat since the 1998-2000 Yankees and only the fifth in MLB history (Athletics 1972-74; Yankees 1949-53; Yankees 1936-39). Instead, they’ll turn their attention to the off-season, with Hernandez, Miguel Rojas, Alex Vesia and, most notably, Tarik Skubal all headed for free agency.
Before then, the Brewers will participate in a World Series featuring two of MLB’s lowest payrolls, undermining the narrative that MLB needs a salary cap for small-market teams to compete. The Brewers didn’t just beat the Dodgers, they dominated them thanks to elite player acquisition, strong player development and a strong team culture.
Soon enough, more tests await the Brewers. First, though, it’s time for a well deserved celebration.

item.title: [Heavy.com] Dodgers Gamble On Ex-Tigers Pitcher Tarik Skubal Backfires

item.description: Earlier this season, the Detroit Tigers made the difficult decision to part ways with ace pitcher Tarik Skubal, sending him to the defending World Series champion Los Angeles Dodgers in return for a package that included a trio of prospects. While the Tigers missed the playoffs, the Dodgers once again advanced to the National League Championship Series, but their dreams of a three-peat were broken by the upstart Milwaukee Brewers. In a stunning result, the Brewers swept Tarik Skubal and the Dodg
item.content:encoded:
Earlier this season, the Detroit Tigers made the difficult decision to part ways with ace pitcher Tarik Skubal, sending him to the defending World Series champion Los Angeles Dodgers in return for a package that included a trio of prospects.
While the Tigers missed the playoffs, the Dodgers once again advanced to the National League Championship Series, but their dreams of a three-peat were broken by the upstart Milwaukee Brewers.
In a stunning result, the Brewers swept Tarik Skubal and the Dodgers in four games, advancing to the World Series for the first time since 1982.
Former Detroit Tigers Ace Tarik Skubal And The Los Angeles Dodgers Were Swept In The NLCS
The run for Skubal and the Dodgers this season ended in extreme disappointment, as the New York Yankees remain the most recent club to capture three straight World Series wins.
It was Skubal who started the first game of the NLCS against the Brewers; while he delivered an acceptable performance, he didn’t get much run support. He allowed just two earned runs on five hits and two walks with seven strikeouts over 5.0 innings of work in what was a 2-1 loss.
Now, the Dodgers are faced with an uncertain future with regard to Skubal, who can become an unrestricted free agent and is expected to command a historic contract negotiated by power agent Scott Boras potentially worth upward of $400 million.
Whether or not the Dodgers are able to keep Skubal remains to be seen.
The Tigers Traded Tarik Skubal To The Dodgers
In return for Skubal, the Tigers received outfielder Zyhir Hope and right-handers River Ryan and Brady Smith.
“We came into this with a firm idea of the type of deal that we wanted to ultimately land,” said Tigers executive Scott Harris after the trade. “And we had a deep understanding of what every organization had to offer.
“I think there is a unique dynamic with a player like Tarik Skubal. Markets at the deadline for the top players are just different than the rest of the market. So, I understand the intuition that, ‘Hey, you’re supposed to wait until the very last second on a deal and then pull a trigger at the very last second to maximize a return.’ That’s not how markets for the top players work.”

item.content:encoded:
Dodgers’ manager Dave Roberts told reporters on Thursday that he’s very unlikely to use Tarik Skubal or Yoshinobu Yamamoto out of the bullpen in Game 4 of the NLCS against the Brewers.

Even with their backs against the wall, Roberts maintained confidence when asked if his star hurlers would be available out of the bullpen on Thursday, saying, “No. ... Our bullpen is rested, very, very capable. You’ve still got to win four, but obviously you’ve got to win one first, and I completely understand that. But the short answer, no.” It’s possible that the calculus could change if the Dodgers get down early in Game 4, but for now he appears to have full faith in Tyler Glasnow and his rested bullpen.

item.title: [Reviewing the Brew] Everything Brewers fans need to know about Dodgers’ Game 4 starter Tyler Glasnow

Alas, the Crew will have to get through Tyler Glasnow if they want to complete their revenge arc and sweep the two-time reigning champs in the NLCS.
