item.content:encoded:
It's sort of a sick joke that, even down 3-0 and having used up their trio of all-universe aces, the Los Angeles Dodgers can trot another frontline starter out to the mound to try and stave off elimination against the Milwaukee Brewers. Alas, the Crew will have to get through Tyler Glasnow if they want to complete their revenge arc and sweep the two-time reigning champs in the NLCS.
Of course, after seeing Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, and Blake Snell -- who have four Cy Youngs and a World Series MVP between them -- there's not much that should faze the Brewers. Glasnow is a very good pitcher, but he's the closest thing to a weak link in the Dodgers' super-rotation.
Still, he's an intimidating presence on the bump and has had tons of success against most of Pat Murphy's lineup to boot. Milwaukee will counter with rookie southpaw Shane Drohan, though this will be an all-hands-on-deck effort as the Brewers try to get to where they haven't been since 1982.
To sweep Dodgers, Brewers will need to overcome intimidating history against Tyler Glasnow
Let's start with the optimistic view. Glasnow remains a perpetually injury-prone pitcher, making just 13 starts this year while dealing with back spasms and various setbacks. Though that means his arm should be fresh, he also likely isn't operating at 100%; his last start (against the Braves in the NLDS) saw him yield only one hit across 4⅔ innings, but he also walked five batters as part of a laborious outing.
That's an exploitable weakness the Crew need to take advantage of, since Glasnow has walked multiple batters in each of his past five starts. Running up his pitch count early will force Dave Roberts to dig into his stash of relievers, many of whom seemingly don't have his trust right now.
The major concern for the Brewers lies in the past, since Glasnow has had their number historically. Christian Yelich (one hit, seven strikeouts in 14 plate appearances), William Contreras (zero hits in 10 PAs), and Jackson Chourio (.286 OPS in seven PAs) have all struggled mightily in their head-to-head matchups with the right-hander.
Those numbers also don't include his dominant performance in Game 3 of last year's NLCS, when he struck out eight and held the Brewers to one run on three hits over 5⅔ innings. As such, the work of Game 3 hero Jake Bauers (.952 OPS in seven PAs) and Brice Turang (.375 OBP in eight PAs) will be key to getting the Crew ahead tonight.
Having already taken down all of the Dodgers' best arms, the Brewers should enter this one with immense confidence. With a trip to the World Series on the line, all they need to do is crush their Tyler Glasnow demons.

item.title: [Motor City Bengals] Checking in on the Tigers' Tarik Skubal return as the Dodgers stare down elimination
item.dc:creator: Anthony Ranaudo
item.description: It's bittersweet to watch someone you loved for so long pitch in October for another team, especially one that could win a championship. Tarik Skubal won two Cy Youngs in a Tigers uniform, and now he's chasing a ring with the Dodgers, who trail the Brewers 3-0 in the NLCS. LA needs three wins in a row just to get to a Game 7, and a fourth just to get to the World Series. It's a steep climb, and if it ends this week, the conversation in Detroit shifts quickly from what was lost to what was gained
item.content:encoded:
It's bittersweet to watch someone you loved for so long pitch in October for another team, especially one that could win a championship. Tarik Skubal won two Cy Youngs in a Tigers uniform, and now he's chasing a ring with the Dodgers, who trail the Brewers 3-0 in the NLCS.
LA needs three wins in a row just to get to a Game 7, and a fourth just to get to the World Series. It's a steep climb, and if it ends this week, the conversation in Detroit shifts quickly from what was lost to what was gained.
How the Tigers' Skubal trade return looks heading into 2027
The package was Zyhir Hope, River Ryan and Brady Smith, and each one is in a different place right now, starting with the centerpiece. Hope recently kicked off his stint in the highly-touted Arizona Fall League, and is off to a nice start. Through six games with Scottsdale he's hitting .286 with an .873 OPS, five walks, eight strikeouts and five RBI. He hit his first homer on Monday, a two-run shot at 101 MPH.
However, it wasn't all smooth at the outset for Hope when he was traded over. MLB.com noted he had "plenty of adjusting to do" with a new organization and lineup, and after a very slow start, his Double-A line with Erie (.269/.360/.462) wound up being not as pretty as what he'd done at Tulsa (.293/.369/.530). He crushed the ball in September and still wrapped up the 2026 season with 29 homers, 26 steals and 111 RBI, and went deep in the Eastern League finals.
This AFL start is a small sample (and will be, no matter how good or bad it goes), especially after a career-high 564 plate appearances, but it's an encouraging sign. As for 2027, there's a lot of excitement around the organization about how he can contribute, and when he will arrive in Detroit. Still, it's worth not piling expectations on a young player. Time will tell, and the Tigers will give him plenty of opportunity.
The most immediate return is River Ryan, who has already pitched for the big-league club. He debuted on September 21 with three scoreless innings against the Nationals, and closed the year with a 4.15 ERA and six strikeouts over 4⅓ innings in two starts. That's a tiny sample, so the numbers behind it are worth a look. He throws six pitches, and all of them are average or above average according to Stuff+. And he commands them: in Triple-A this year he struck out 10.3 per nine while walking just 2.0.
There may be some injury concern as he's coming back from Tommy John surgery and a hamstring injury this past year, and really since 2024. And although it was that small sample size, his two MLB starts included 6.2 walks per nine, which is a bit alarming. But his lengthy Triple-A numbers make me feel better. No matter what, the stuff and the strike-throwing are why people are excited, and if he stays healthy he should be penciled into the 2027 rotation.
Health is also the story with Smith. He made two starts for High-A West Michigan before leaving his second in the second inning after five batters and a visit from a trainer, and he went on the injured list August 20. With Tommy John surgery in his past, I'd bet they shut him down as a precaution and are aiming for a healthy 2027. If he is, I'd expect him to move up to Double-A at some point, and since he came over in the Skubal trade, the organization should give him plenty of runway to get to the big leagues.
That's the thing about this trade. It's fun to watch Skubal even when it hurts to see him in another uniform, but between Hope's bat, Ryan's arm and Smith's upside, the 2027-and-beyond picture is exciting too. And if the Dodgers can't manage a comeback, it's even sweeter.

item.title: [reviewingthebrew.com] Brewers' best (and only) chance for historic playoff redemption in NLCS is in Shane Drohan's hands

With a pair of Cy Young-winning left-handers in Tarik Skubal, whom the Dodgers acquired at the midseason trade deadline, and Blake Snell, as well as 2025 World Series MVP Yoshinobu Yamamoto and All-Star right-hander Tyler Glasnow in their rotation, that attention was well-deserved. item.content:encoded:
Much of the media's attention heading into this year's NLCS rematch between the Milwaukee Brewers and Los Angeles Dodgers was on the strength of the defending World Series Champions' starting pitching group. With a pair of Cy Young-winning left-handers in Tarik Skubal, whom the Dodgers acquired at the midseason trade deadline, and Blake Snell, as well as 2025 World Series MVP Yoshinobu Yamamoto and All-Star right-hander Tyler Glasnow in their rotation, that attention was well-deserved.
However, through the first three games of the NLCS, the Brewers have bested Los Angeles' top three starters and built a commanding 3-0 series lead. Skubal and Snell took the loss in Games 1 and 3, respectively, and sandwiched in between was a 2.2-inning, 75-pitch start from Yamamoto that forced Dave Roberts to use seven relief pitchers in Game 2. On the other side, Milwaukee's starting group hasn't necessarily been the strength of their pitching staff during the postseason -- that would be their bullpen -- but the trio of Jacob Misiorowski, Logan Henderson, and Robert Gasser combined for 13.1 innings and allowed just two earned runs through the first three NLCS games.
Game 4 is where things get interesting. While the Brewers' decision to start Miz, Henderson, and Gasser in the first three games of the NLCS felt like an obvious one, especially after Gasser's strong showing in the NLDS, who would get the ball to start Game 4 remained an unanswered question through this morning.
However, just moments ago, the Brewers officially revealed that rookie southpaw Shane Drohan will start Game 4 of the NLCS tonight. Drohan, who will be making his postseason debut, will be the first out-getter of Milwaukee's quest for never-before-seen level of redemption in a playoff series.
Brewers trying to become first team in MLB history to sweep a team in the playoffs who swept them in the previous postseason
The Brewers just have to win one of their next four games to return to the World Series for the first time since 1982. That much is true. That said, closing out the Dodgers tonight and completing one of the most impressive sweeps in postseason history would be a redemption performance never before seen in MLB history. According to MLB.com's statistician Sarah Langs, no team in the history of MLB has swept a team in a postseason series after being swept by that same team in the previous playoffs.
After the demoralizing loss that the Brewers suffered in last year's NLCS, defeating the Dodgers in four games this year would easily be one of the most satisfying postseason series sweeps in MLB history. Pair that with the payroll disparity that exists between the two clubs, the fact that Los Angeles is pursuing a three-peat, and the Dodgers' victory in the Tarik Skubal trade deadline sweepstakes, and the Brewers sweeping MLB's Evil Empire would be especially gratifying.
Completing that sweep in Game 4 tonight starts with a strong showing from Drohan, who hasn't pitched in any of the Brewers' first seven postseason games this year. Drohan impressed during the regular season, with a 4.19 ERA in 124.2 innings to prove it. His low arm-slot from the left side matches up well with Shohei Ohtani and Freddie Freeman, and his six-pitch mix should keep the struggling Dodgers' offense off-balance.
It likely won't be a long start for Drohan, especially given the arms available in Pat Murphy's 'pen. In theory, only DL Hall is unavailable for tonight's game, but the Brewers may elect to avoid using Abner Uribe for an eighth consecutive game as well. However, that leaves Kyle Harrison, Dustin May, Chad Patrick, Aaron Ashby, Antonio Senzatela, JoJo Romero, and Trevor Megill available for Murphy to turn to after Drohan.
Any type of victory over the Dodgers in this year's NLCS would represent redemption for the Brewers after being swept by Los Angeles a season ago. However, Milwaukee's only shot at historic redemption that has never occurred in the history of MLB is tonight, during which rookie southpaw Shane Drohan will kick off their sweep attempt.

item.title: [si.com] Brewers Are Using Postseason Stage to Showcase MLB’s New Era
item.dc:creator: Tom Verducci
item.description: Los Angeles — When dynasties fall, it is not insurrection, nor jealousy, nor sloth that bring them down. It is the undefeated champion of the world, Father Time. We are watching the Los Angeles Dodgers age out. The Milwaukee Brewers proved for a third time in the National League Championship Series they are the better (and younger) team, completing a beautiful triptych of comebacks with a 6-2 win in Game 3 on Wednesday. In three successive games, the Dodgers had Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto
item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles — When dynasties fall, it is not insurrection, nor jealousy, nor sloth that bring them down. It is the undefeated champion of the world, Father Time. We are watching the Los Angeles Dodgers age out.
The Milwaukee Brewers proved for a third time in the National League Championship Series they are the better (and younger) team, completing a beautiful triptych of comebacks with a 6-2 win in Game 3 on Wednesday. In three successive games, the Dodgers had Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Blake Snell on the mound with a lead and lost all three. Ninety-five million dollars, four Cy Young awards and a World Series MVP worth of pitching and they could not hold back Milwaukee any more than you can hold back water with your hands.
But the most obvious reason why the Brewers have put the Dodger dynasty on the brink of extinction is this: the youngest pitching staff in baseball—and the hardest throwing staff in postseason history—has smothered the oldest team in baseball. Milwaukee is pushing around the aging Dodgers lineup with a barrage of fastballs in three versions, especially power sinkers. They are shoving 66.8% fastballs at the Dodgers at an average velocity of 97.9 mph. The Dodgers’ only path to victory is to slug and the Brewers simply won’t allow it.
“I just think they’re really good pitchers,” Dodgers infielder Miguel Rojas said. “A lot of their pitchers throw three different fastballs. They throw hard, and they’ve been locating the ball really well. They haven’t really given us too much of an opportunity to kind of build momentum.
“They’ve been attacking the zone. They throw their stuff in the zone—and with all three fastballs. A lot of guys have a cutter, a sinker and a four-seam fastball. It’s really hard to put barrels on the ball.
“At the end of the day, it’s just the velocity of their stuff. They throw the ball really hard. And we all know when you throw that hard, it’s really hard.”
The Brewers knew coming into the series that in today’s game older players don’t hit elite fastballs as well as younger players, and so the matchup was to their liking. But this? Who could have seen this in the NLCS? The Dodgers:
- Have two extra-base hits in 105 plate appearances
- Have been outhomered, 5-0
- Are the first team in franchise history to lose three straight games in one postseason with no home runs and no attempted stolen bases
- Are hitting .228 against fastballs
- Are 2-for-16 with runners in scoring position, part of a 3-for-32 postseason disaster in those spots
This has been the year in which baseball made a sharp turn when it comes to the speed of the game. Younger players thrive. Velocity, and the widespread adoption of the family of three fastballs, changed everything. You need fast-twitch athleticism, youthfulness. You need this generation of players who know velocity as a first language. You need rangy players on defense. The numbers bear out that younger players are the preferred way to go.
Players 30 and younger this year hit .247. Players in the 31-35 year-old demographic hit 10 points worse, .237, their worst showing ever. There was a time when front offices valued those 31-35 players because it seemed to be the peak intersection of experience and physical tools. Front offices were afraid to commit to younger players because of the lack of reps and track records. Those days are over.
The difference on the field in NLCS Game 3 was striking. The Brewers are the fastest team in baseball, as measured by sprint speed. The Dodgers are 24th.
The Brewers started a lineup and a pitcher with an average age of 26.1. They became the first team in history with a second postseason game starting three players 22 and younger: leftfielder Jackson Chourio, shortstop Cooper Pratt and rightfielder Luis Lara. Chourio opened the game with a first-pitch homer. Pratt smacked three hits, stole a base and scored a run. Lara flew around rightfield like a bird of prey, snaring anything that dared enter his airspace.
Watching Chourio, 22, Garrett Mitchell, 28, and Lara, 21, patrol the outfield was like watching an Olympic sprint relay team.
On the other side of the field, the Dodgers, especially their bats, looked old and slow. The average age of their starting 10 was 32.3 years old—more than six years older than Milwaukee’s fearless group. Only two starting Dodgers were in their 20s: centerfielder Andy Pages, 25, and Kyle Tucker, 29, who with his diminished range and baserunning has been trending older than his age.
By starting eight players 31 and older, these Dodgers joined the 2023 Dodgers, who got bounced by the Diamondbacks, as the only teams in the past 19 postseasons to trot out so many starting players that old in a game.
Fittingly, the old team played an outdated style of baseball, one from a generation ago. The ninth-place hitter, Tommy Edman, twice batted after the leadoff runner reached first base. Twice manager Dave Roberts did not ask him to bunt.
“I thought about it, but it’s just, he had a good pitch to hit. Flew out,” Roberts said. “I just didn’t feel giving up an out right there. Early in the game, I wanted Tommy to hit ...
“We haven’t been getting hits with runners in scoring position. To give up an out, to bank on getting a hit with runners in scoring position, I’d rather just try to maybe slug, hit a double.”
Edman was a below average hitter (97 OPS+) with a .385 slug this season.
Roberts and the Dodgers keep waiting for slug to show up at the expense of forfeiting the situational baseball as deployed by the other three remaining teams, the youthful Brewers, Guardians and Rays. The Dodgers still may be waiting Thanksgiving morning.
For instance, the Dodgers were down 1-0 in the sixth when Roberts sent 36-year-old Max Muncy to hit for Pages with runners on first and second and no outs. In that situation, the Brewers are bunting. Milwaukee plays get-em-over, get-em-in ball. The Dodgers? No way. Muncy is a three-true outcome guy. He is not going to bunt. Again, the Dodgers played for slug and got nothing. Muncy struck out. Will Smith, 31, did save the rally with a two-run double. But the Dodgers would go 1-for-12 after that against hard-throwing relievers D.L. Hall and Trevor Megill.
The lineup remained cold. Shohei Ohtani, 32, cannot pull a baseball because of lower-half injuries that won’t allow him to properly turn his hips and get to a firm front side. Freeman, 37, has three extra-base hits since Aug. 31.
“[Our] pitching staff has been great, to be honest,” Rojas said. “It’s really hard to put it into context when you have to pitch and have to play defense with a one run lead every single time. It’s like asking these guys to just throw a perfect inning every single time. It’s not sustainable. So, the blame is on the offense. We all know we could’ve done better, but nothing we can do now.”
How in the world has Milwaukee made Los Angeles look so bad?
“It’s pretty simple,” Muncy said. “We’ve played like [poop]. They’ve played great.”
Occam’s razor (or commode) aside, the one-sided NLCS is bigger than that. It stands as a changing of the guard, recalling the 1964 World Series, when the St. Louis Cardinals, emblematic of the National League embracing Black and Latin American players, ended the dynasty of an aging New York Yankees team, then the second oldest team in baseball. The younger, faster, harder-throwing, more creative team has been, beyond doubt, the better team.
Tom Verducci is a senior writer for Sports Illustrated who has covered Major League Baseball since 1981. He also serves as an analyst for FOX Sports and the MLB Network; is a New York Times best-selling author; and cohosts The Book of Joe podcast with Joe Maddon. A five-time Emmy Award winner across three categories (studio analyst, reporter, short form writing) and nominated in a fourth (game analyst), he is a three-time National Sportswriter of the Year winner, two-time National Magazine Award finalist, and a Penn State Distinguished Alumnus Award recipient. Verducci is a member of the National Sports Media Hall of Fame, Baseball Writers Association of America (including past New York chapter chairman) and a Baseball Hall of Fame voter since 1993. He also is the only writer to be a game analyst for World Series telecasts. He lives in New Jersey with his wife, with whom he has two children.

item.title: [Heavy.com] What Dodgers' Dave Roberts Said About Being Down 3-0 in NLCS
item.dc:creator: Curt Bishop
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers are on the brink of elimination. With a 6-2 loss in Game 3 of the National League Championship Series, they are at risk of being swept by the Milwaukee Brewers and watching their chances of a three-peat be dashed. Manager Dave Roberts has been in this position before as a player. In 2004, the Boston Red Sox faced a 3-0 deficit in the American League Championship Series before rallying to win four games in a row and knock out the New York Yankees before sweeping the St. Lo
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are on the brink of elimination. With a 6-2 loss in Game 3 of the National League Championship Series, they are at risk of being swept by the Milwaukee Brewers and watching their chances of a three-peat be dashed.
Manager Dave Roberts has been in this position before as a player. In 2004, the Boston Red Sox faced a 3-0 deficit in the American League Championship Series before rallying to win four games in a row and knock out the New York Yankees before sweeping the St. Louis Cardinals in the World Series. A key stolen base by Roberts in the ninth inning of Game 4 sparked the comeback.
However, after Game 3 of the NLCS, Roberts was asked about the 2004 comeback and made clear that that is not his focus heading into Game 4 against the Brewers.
“They’ve all seen the documentary, so they know it can happen,” Roberts said.
Dave Roberts Weighs in on 2004 ALCS Comeback
It has been 22 years since the Red Sox pulled off their comeback against the Yankees. They were three outs away from being swept out of the playoffs by the Yankees.
Roberts obviously played a key role in that as a player with his stolen base. But the point he makes is that what happened in 2004 is irrelevant. The Dodgers are in the exact same spot as the Red Sox were, but to win this series, the focus isn’t going to be on the past, but rather, what they can do to chip away at the Brewers.
No two situations are going to play out exactly the same, even though the Dodgers are in the same position the Red Sox were all those years ago, this potential comeback will look a lot different.
Things are not looking good for the Dodgers, but Roberts made clear that he doesn’t want his team to dwell on the past and try to find inspiration in something that took place 22 years ago.
What that series proved is that it’s always possible for the unexpected to happen, and it is a reminder that it’s never over until it’s over. But that was a long time ago. The Dodgers have business to take care of and cannot afford to get lost in the past and try to replicate what was done.
They’re going to have to do it their own way. They have won back-to-back World Series titles after all, so there is certainly still some hope.
What’s Next for Los Angeles Dodgers After Game 3 Loss?
The Dodgers have already announced Tyler Glasnow as their Game 4 starter. If they win Game 4, they’ll get the ball back in Tarik Skubal’s hands for Game 5. Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Blake Snell would be next in line for Games 6 and 7 if the series gets that far. One win could potentially give the Dodgers a little bit of momentum as they try to get back to the World Series and stave off elimination, but there is a lot of momentum that they are already up against as they head into Game 4.

His answer was no, leaving Los Angeles to pursue a comeback without either pitcher as a relief option. The decision comes afte
item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts has ruled out using Tarik Skubal or Yoshinobu Yamamoto in relief for Thursday's must-win Game 4 of the National League Championship Series against the Milwaukee Brewers.
According to Ben Nicholson-Smith of Sportsnet, Roberts was asked whether either starter could be available out of the bullpen with the Dodgers facing elimination. His answer was no, leaving Los Angeles to pursue a comeback without either pitcher as a relief option.
The decision comes after Milwaukee defeated Los Angeles 6-2 in Game 3 on Wednesday, pushing the Dodgers into a 3-0 series deficit. The Brewers are now one win away from reaching the World Series for the first time since 1982.
Skubal started Game 1 of the series and allowed two runs over five innings, recording seven strikeouts and two walks. The Dodgers lost that game 2-1, putting the pressure on their rotation early in the series.
Yamamoto started Game 2 but struggled to work deep into the contest. He allowed three runs on four hits and two walks over 2 2/3 innings as Milwaukee secured a 7-4 victory. The right-hander had been named the 2025 World Series MVP after helping Los Angeles win the championship.
The Dodgers entered the postseason after finishing the regular season 100-62, while Milwaukee went 103-59 to earn the National League's top seed. The Brewers have carried that form into the NLCS, winning the first three games and limiting Los Angeles' margin for error.
Tyler Glasnow is scheduled to start Game 4 for the Dodgers. He pitched 4 2/3 innings of one-run baseball in the NLDS-clinching win over the Atlanta Braves, although he issued five walks in that appearance.
The Dodgers must win four consecutive games to advance, beginning Thursday at Dodger Stadium. Only the 2004 Boston Red Sox have overcome a 3-0 deficit to win a best-of-seven MLB postseason series.
Roberts' decision means Los Angeles will need Glasnow and its available bullpen arms to handle the elimination game. Milwaukee, meanwhile, can clinch the NLCS and secure its first World Series berth since 1982 with another victory.
This story was originally published by Athlon on Oct 15, 2026, where it first appeared in the MLB section. Add Athlon as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

item.title: [Dodgers Way] Miguel Rojas is getting rightfully roasted for fate-tempting cleats as Dodgers go down 3-0

item.content:encoded:
These Los Angeles Dodgers broke a 25-year streak by becoming the first back-to-back champions with the World Series victory over the Toronto Blue Jays last year.
Since then, all the talk about from the national media has been whether or not they could follow that 1998-2000 New York Yankees squad into the hallowed halls of three-peaters.
Down 2-0 to the Brewers in the NLCS, however, the goal of Game 3 was merely about survival. Which is why Miguel Rojas' cleats suggesting that a third title is on the horizon has naturally garnered quite a lot of attention on social media.
Now faced with the prospect of having to win four games in a row to even advance to the World Series, baseball fans may be waiting for that three-peat to load for quite a long time.
Dodgers have been humbled by Brewers, but they're equipped to make an improbable NLCS comeback
Because the Dodgers have been so dominant for so long, fans of other teams rarely miss their chance dunk on Los Angeles when the opportunity presents itself.
The good news for the Dodgers is that this series isn't over. A 3-0 deficit is daunting, but they're better equipped than most to come back from it. Tyler Glasnow will take the ball tonight against old friend Dustin May, giving Dave Roberts a clear advantage on the mound from the get-go.
If the Dodgers able to stave off the sweep at Chavez Ravine, they'll get one more game at home, this time with Tarik Skubal on the mound. Then, Game 6 in Milwaukee would allow them to deploy Yoshinobu Yamamoto again. After that would come a do-or-die Game 7 with Blake Snell eyeing a chance at redemption after Jake Bauers got the better of him last night.
That's a lot of looking ahead for a team that hasn't won a game in the NLCS to date, but it's a reminder of how stacked this roster is. Even with Jacob Misiorowski waiting in the wings, you'd have to like the Dodgers' chances of winning with Skubal and Yamamoto on the mound if they can get to their next starts.
It all starts with getting back in win column tonight and delaying the inevitable for another day. Failing that, Rojas may need to find the nearest dumpster in which to deposit his custom cleats.

item.title: [amNewYork] Mets rumors: Is Tarik Skubal a legitimate target? | amNewYork
item.dc:creator: Joe Pantorno; Amnewyork

Zac Thornton spoke with Mike Puma of the New York Post earlier this week and admitted that it’s a hot topic of conversation with his teammates. “I talk to [Nolan McLean] all the time about it, and he had some good talks with Skubal when they were in the [World Baseball Classic] together,” Thornton told Puma. “It would be awesome to bounce ideas, especial
item.content:encoded:
The prospect of Tarik Skubal becoming the Mets’ next big free-agent signing is already dancing in the head of some members of the organization.
Zac Thornton spoke with Mike Puma of the New York Post earlier this week and admitted that it’s a hot topic of conversation with his teammates.
“I talk to [Nolan McLean] all the time about it, and he had some good talks with Skubal when they were in the [World Baseball Classic] together,” Thornton told Puma. “It would be awesome to bounce ideas, especially coming from another left-handed pitcher. Sean [Manaea] and I talk a lot, just about being lefties — there are not many around here, so it would be awesome to have another powerhouse left-handed pitcher around here.”
Even with a young core of promising arms like McLean, Thornton, Christian Scott, and Jonah Tong, president of baseball operations David Stearns made it clear in his end-of-season availability that “it is necessary for us to add to our rotation.”
Skubal would provide the bona fide veteran ace Freddy Peralta never became after his half season in Queens—though he certainly looks the part with the Tampa Bay Rays, who are battling the Cleveland Guardians in the ALCS.
Regardless, the left-handed Skubal will be the crown jewel of the free agent market this winter. The two-time defending American League Cy Young Award winner was dealt from the Detroit Tigers to the Los Angeles Dodgers at the trade deadline and remained his dominant self, going 5-2 with a 2.61 ERA and 1.048 WHIP.
Over his last three seasons, Skubal is 43-17 with a 2.42 ERA and 655 strikeouts in 546 innings pitched.
With a lockout looming, which could potentially carry a salary cap that will limit player salaries, Skubal will likely sign quickly — and that deal will be historic. He is projected to sign the richest contract for a free-agent pitcher ever, which should exceed $300 million.
Whether Stearns would be intrigued by doling out such an offer might not be as cut-and-dry as many might initially think.
Yes, the Mets’ president of baseball operations has had an aversion to handing out long-term big-money contracts to pitchers, which is understandable given the fragility of many major-league arms and the seemingly never-ending onslaught of injuries that come with it.
Skubal himself missed a month earlier this season when he had to undergo surgery to remove loose bodies from his pitching elbow.
But Stearns has gone to the negotiating table with a big-money contract offer for a starting pitcher while with the Mets. He offered Yoshinobu Yamamoto a 12-year, $325 million deal in December of 2023, but the Japanese superstar took an identical deal to join the Los Angeles Dodgers.
Skubal would certainly fit the mold of coaxing such an offer from Stearns, especially if it means that the Mets are that much closer to legitimate contention in 2027, if there is baseball.

item.title: [FanSided] 3 mistakes the Dodgers made with their money that cost them a chance at a three-peat
item.dc:creator: Zachary Rotman
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers have won back-to-back World Series titles thanks largely to historic spending. item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers have won back-to-back World Series titles thanks largely to historic spending. A full14 players on the Dodgers' roster are making eight figures this season, and Tarik Skubal (who is making $32 million overall, but $9.5 million prorated after the Dodgers acquired him) isn't far behind from making that 15. For reference, the Mets, the team closest to L.A. payroll-wise, ended the year with just eight players making eight figures this season.
Most of those deals are ones the Dodgers would sign off on again. Even guys who have struggled this postseason, like Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts, Shohei Ohtani and Will Smith, have done so much for this team in recent years that it's hard to say the Dodgers should regret paying them. These three deals, though, are ones that the Dodgers should regret offering, now that their three-peat dreams are officially on life support.
OF Kyle Tucker
This is the obvious one. The Dodgers, even after winning back-to-back World Series titles, elected to give Kyle Tucker a four-year, $240 million deal in free agency. When that deal was signed, most MLB fans practically handed the World Series title to L.A., knowing how good Tucker had been in Houston. Instead, Tucker wound up having the worst year of his career.
He slashed .233/.330/.385 with 17 home runs and 70 RBI. He was better down the stretch and has been arguably their best hitter in the postseason, but he's just 2-for-8 in the NLCS. That's not good enough for a player making $60 million a year on average. For reference, Juan Soto's AAV is at $51 million, and he's performed at an MVP level. If the Dodgers got to do it again, they almost certainly wouldn't have made this kind of investment in Tucker.
RHP Edwin Diaz
Tucker wasn't the only high-end free agent the Dodgers signed. They gave Edwin Diaz a three-year, $69 million deal to be their closer, one year after giving Tanner Scott a four-year, $72 million deal to perform in that same role. Scott's first year in L.A. was one to forget, and Diaz followed that same path, posting an 8.68 ERA in 21 games and missing much of the season due to injury.
Diaz was better in the postseason, but given how well Scott performed this season and how lackluster this Dodgers lineup proved to be, wouldn't Andrew Friedman have preferred to give that kind of major money to a big bat? Hindsight is 20/20, but had they known the offense would look this bad in October, they likely would've spent their resources on another bat and let Diaz sign elsewhere.
OF Teoscar Hernandez
Teoscar Hernandez had a huge year in 2024, leading to the Dodgers re-signing him on a three-year, $66 million deal that offseason. That contract made some sense, but handing a power-hitting corner outfielder over the age of 30 a hefty multi-year deal has the risk of backfiring — and this one did almost immediately. Hernandez's 103 OPS+ in 2025 was his worst in a full season in his career, and while he was a bit better overall in 2026, his streakiness and his numbers against righties (.695 OPS) left a lot to be desired.
Those struggles have continued into the playoffs, with Hernandez going 5-for-26 overall and 2-for-10 in the NLCS thus far. Dave Roberts has consistently hit him in the heart of the Dodgers' order, but Hernandez has not been able to come through. There're plenty of other players making the $20+ million that Hernandez is who could've come through for L.A. offensively. With another guaranteed year on his deal, this contract feels like another one that the Dodgers regret.

item.title: [Heavy.com] Ex-Tigers Ace Tarik Skubal Comes Clean On Major Pressure With Dodgers
item.dc:creator: Michael Whitaker
item.description: In early August, the Detroit Tigers put to rest any idea of extending ace pitcher Tarik Skubal, who was dealt to the Los Angeles Dodgers in return for a trio of prospects, which included pitcher River Ryan. While the Tigers unfortunately failed to earn a spot in the MLB postseason, the Dodgers are back in the National League Championship Series once again. And Skubal is attempting to help the club become the first team in over a quarter-century to win three straight World Series titles. Former D
item.content:encoded:
In early August, the Detroit Tigers put to rest any idea of extending ace pitcher Tarik Skubal, who was dealt to the Los Angeles Dodgers in return for a trio of prospects, which included pitcher River Ryan.
While the Tigers unfortunately failed to earn a spot in the MLB postseason, the Dodgers are back in the National League Championship Series once again. And Skubal is attempting to help the club become the first team in over a quarter-century to win three straight World Series titles.
Former Detroit Tigers Pitcher Tarik Skubal Comes Clean On Heavy Expectations
Given his status as one of the premier players at his position in baseball, along with what the Dodgers are trying to accomplish, Skubal is well aware of the heavy expectations that he’s facing.
However, he made it clear that he embraces it.
“The pressure surrounding the Dodgers is a privilege. As an athlete, this is what you want to be and you want to have an expectation to win,” Skubal said to Dodgers Nation’s Noel Sanchez.
“I have those same expectations as a player and in my shoes, I think just keeping the game the game, going out there and competing and doing what I can to put my team in a position to win is important.”
Despite a good performance on the mound against the Brewers in Game 1 of the NLCS, Skubal was credited with the loss; his next starting opportunity is Game 5, but he and his teammates currently trail two games to none.
It Was Not Easy For The Tigers To Lose Tarik Skubal
Shortly after the trade of Skubal to the Dodgers was completed, Tigers manager A.J. Hinch admitted that it wasn’t easy despite having been preparing for that potential outcome.
“We’ve been bracing for something like this to happen,” Hinch said of the trade via the Detroit News. “Even though we’ve been talking about it for a couple of months, it’s still tough when it becomes a reality. But these guys are pretty resilient.”
“It’s been incredible to watch this guy rise to the top of the sport,” Hinch said. “He carried us a lot and I am forever grateful that our paths crossed. And for the things he did for this organization and the two playoff teams. His presence, his work ethic, his example, his dominance, there’s just so much to go through. But I am very grateful I was able to manage him for the time I did.”

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are looking to climb out of a 0-2 hole against the Milwaukee Brewers as the National League Championship Series shifts to Hollywood on Wednesday night.
The Brewers scratched out a 2-1 win in Game 1 before taking Game 2 by a final score of 7-4 at home. However, Milwaukee hasn’t been the same team on the road this season, and the Dodgers are obviously a team with playoff experience.
I have a pick and a prop for Dodgers vs. Brewers in NLCS Game 3 on Wednesday night.
Let’s get right into the MLB best bets – and their odds at the best betting sites – for Wednesday, Oct. 14.
MLB Best Bets for Wednesday, Oct. 14
- Dodgers -1.5 (+129) vs. Brewers
- Blake Snell UNDER 1.5 Earned Runs (-133)
Dodgers -1.5 (+129) vs. Brewers
I explained in the NLCS Game 3 betting preview why I like the Dodgers to get in the win column tonight:
The Brewers were able to maintain their home-field advantage in the first two games of the series, and I think the Dodgers will get a win at home in Game 3.
This is where the Dodgers’ depth really shows. Blake Snell would be the Game 1 or at least Game 2 starter for most teams, but Los Angeles’ acquisition of Tarik Skubal at the trade deadline pushes the veteran southpaw to Game 3 at home.
Robert Gasser has been better than people think for Milwaukee, but I’m not too sure he can go toe-to-toe with Snell. And if the Brewers get a lead, the Brewers would be smart to save their best bullpen arms for the rest of the series.
It is a big price for the Dodgers at -180, though, which is why I’m recommending the run line as my best bet. If you want to just take the moneyline, that’s fine too, but I don’t like giving out best bets at this high of a number.
Blake Snell UNDER 1.5 Earned Runs (-133)
I also broke down why I’m backing Blake Snell to silence the Brewers in NLCS Game 3:
Blake Snell has been terrific since returning from the injured list in early August. He allowed five runs in 39.2 innings (1.13 ERA) in his final eight regular-season starts, yielding one run or fewer in all eight outings.
The veteran southpaw then allowed just one run in his start against the Braves in the NLDS.
The Brewers weren’t as good on the road this season, and Snell has been lights out no matter where he’s pitching. In fact, Snell allowed just one run in 18 innings in three starts at Dodger Stadium after returning from the IL.

item.title: [Brewer Fanatic] A Different Kind of Challenge: How Can Brewers Beat Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow?
item.dc:creator: Jake McKibbin
item.description: Brewers Video Tarik Skubal and Yoshinobu Yamamoto are the Dodgers' near-immortal October heroes. After most teams start a series with hurlers like that, there's a major step down in quality to the back half of their rotation. In Los Angeles's case, though, that step is much smaller. Here's how the Brewers can attack the other two-time Cy Young Award winner in the Dodgers rotation, and one of the most physically intimidating pitchers in baseball. Projected Game 3 Starter: Blake Snell The Brewers
item.content:encoded:
Brewers Video
Tarik Skubal and Yoshinobu Yamamoto are the Dodgers' near-immortal October heroes. After most teams start a series with hurlers like that, there's a major step down in quality to the back half of their rotation. In Los Angeles's case, though, that step is much smaller. Here's how the Brewers can attack the other two-time Cy Young Award winner in the Dodgers rotation, and one of the most physically intimidating pitchers in baseball.
Projected Game 3 Starter: Blake Snell
The Brewers got a first-hand look at just how good Snell can be in 2025. He capitalized on a change in his pitch mix, throwing a heavy dose of in-zone changeups that completely befuddled Milwaukee in one of the best starts of his career: eight innings, one hit, 10 strikeouts. But that isn't always the version of Snell that opponents see.
Snell is willing to nibble around the edges of the zone, making swing decisions in the shadow zone particularly important for Milwaukee against another high-release, left-handed pitcher with a devastating fastball and changeup. The difference is that Snell is much more comfortable giving up a walk than Skubal, and somehow even harder to square up when hitters do swing.
His start against the Braves showed both sides of that equation. Snell lasted just 3⅔ innings, walking five hitters and striking out five, but he allowed only one run. Three hits and five walks might suggest that Atlanta simply missed its opportunity, but there is a reason Snell can survive that kind of traffic. His fastball has elite ride, and when he works at the top of the zone, it's extremely difficult to get on top of. Add a wicked slider and curveball that blend beautifully with the fastball from his high release point, plus a quality changeup, and Snell's four-pitch mix is loaded with ways to beat a hitter.
This is the type of contact quality Snell has allowed this season:
Snell isn't overly concerned about the walks, because he trusts his ability to strand runners once they reach base. Especially in the tense environment of a playoff game, he can induce chase, generate swing-and-miss, and force weak contact when hitters finally do get the ball in the zone.
Even when he does throw strikes, Snell is difficult to hit. Fresh off the injured list, his fastball has gained roughly an inch of both ride and run compared with 2025. As a result, the one pitch that hitters had previously been able to barrel with some consistency has taken a step forward.
That makes this a waiting game for Milwaukee. Can the Brewers build enough pressure on Snell that he finally blinks before they do? Can they turn the walks and deep counts into hard contact when he eventually has to come into the zone? More importantly, can they force him to throw enough pitches that the Dodgers have to turn to their bullpen earlier than they'd like?
Atlanta managed to run Snell's pitch count up and get him out of the game, and white-knuckled their way to a win from there. Milwaukee may need a similar approach. They're unlikely to drop the hammer on Snell, and they'll need some batted-ball fortune when their opportunities arrive, but if they can make him work, accept the walks and punish the mistakes, they have a path to turning Snell's greatest strength, his willingness to live on the edges, into a weakness. Braves batters swung at just 34 of the 90 pitches Snell threw in the NLDS. To match that patience in last year's NLCS Game 1, the Brewers would have had to swing 10 fewer times. The key to beating Snell is those 10 fewer swings.
NLCS Game Four Starter: Tyler Glasnow
Tyler Glasnow works from one of the highest release points in baseball, pairing a high-velocity fastball with breaking balls that feature sharp, late movement. Like Snell, he's comfortable working outside the strike zone and using his secondary pitches to induce chases. His two breaking balls can fall off the table, making them difficult to touch—let alone hit hard.
Glasnow threw just 74 innings during the regular season, but posted a 0.95 WHIP and a 34% strikeout rate, a testament to how difficult he is to handle—particularly when he gets ahead in the count. There is, however, another dimension to the matchup. Glasnow can be vulnerable to the running game: opposing runners went 14-for-17 on stolen-base attempts against him in 2026, an 82% success rate. If the Brewers can get men on base, they may have opportunities to pile on pressure with their legs. The bigger question, of course, is how they get on in the first place.
Once again, the fastball could be the key. Glasnow's breaking balls have enough depth and movement to make consistent contact a challenge, particularly when hitters are forced to protect against them outside the strike zone. The Brewers will need to recognise those pitches early and avoid expanding the zone. The encouraging sign is that, unlike Yamamoto, Glasnow has shown a more conventional relationship between count leverage and pitch selection: as he falls behind, the likelihood of seeing a fastball increases.
Glasnow's outing against the Braves offered a glimpse of both his vulnerability and his ability to limit the damage. He struggled to locate his secondary pitches, walking five hitters, and threw his four-seam fastball in the strike zone roughly two-thirds of the time. The Braves managed just one run, however, illustrating how difficult it can be to capitalize on Glasnow's occasional command issues.
Even when Glasnow loses his feel for the secondaries, his four-seamer remains a formidable weapon. Released from a high arm slot, the pitch can play above the barrel, but it also cuts just enough to slide along the barrel. That helps him limit hard contact and keep the ball in the park, even when hitters know a fastball is coming. The offering has some similarities to the one the Brewers recently faced from Nick Pivetta, against whom they timed the fastball well. That being said, recognizing the pitch and actually squaring it up are two very different things.
The Brewers' best approach will be to make Glasnow work. Extending at-bats, laying off pitches outside the zone, and forcing him to find the strike zone with his secondary offerings could create opportunities to get runners aboard. From there, they can look to apply pressure on the bases and turn a difficult matchup into a more uncomfortable one. That fits their broader approach of building pressure and forcing mistakes, but Glasnow is unlikely to unravel simply because the Brewers make him work.
Ultimately, the Brewers will need to combine disciplined at-bats with timely hitting. Glasnow has the stuff to overpower even a patient lineup, and he would be an ace in most postseason rotations. The opportunity is there, but exploiting it will require the Brewers to turn the few openings he gives them into meaningful damage.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers return home in a 2-0 hole against the Milwaukee Brewers in the National League Championship Series.
The Dodgers swept the Brewers last year in the NLCS, but Milwaukee has shown that it won’t go quietly this time around.
Milwaukee won a close battle in Game 1 by a final score of 2-1 before chasing Yoshinobu Yamamoto early in Game 2 in a 7-4 victory.
The Dodgers now return home, where they’re 52-31 this year, while the Brewers are 49-34 on the road.
It’s a southpaw showdown in Hollywood for Game 3 on Wednesday night.
Here are the odds, probable pitchers, and predictions for Brewers vs. Dodgers Game 3 on Wednesday, Oct. 14.
Brewers vs. Dodgers Odds, Run Line and Total
Run Line

- Dodgers -1.5 (+129)
Moneyline

- Dodgers -180
Total
- 7.5 (Over -106/Under -114)

- Brewers: Robert Gasser (5-5, 3.87 ERA)
- Dodgers: Blake Snell (4-1, 1.90 ERA)
Robert Gasser threw four one-run innings against the Dodgers in his first postseason start this year. That run came on a solo home run, one of three hits by the Padres in a 3-1 Brewers victory.
Blake Snell lasted just 3.2 innings in his playoff start against the Braves, allowing one run on three hits with five walks and five strikeouts.

- Dodgers record: 100-62 (3-3)
Brewers vs. Dodgers Best MLB Prop Bets
Dodgers Best MLB Prop Bet
- Blake Snell UNDER 1.5 Earned Runs (-133)
Blake Snell has been terrific since returning from the injured list in early August. He allowed five runs in 39.2 innings (1.13 ERA) in his final eight regular-season starts, yielding one run or fewer in all eight outings.
The veteran southpaw then allowed just one run in his start against the Braves in the NLDS.
The Brewers weren’t as good on the road this season, and Snell has been lights out no matter where he’s pitching. In fact, Snell allowed just one run in 18 innings in three starts at Dodger Stadium after returning from the IL.
Brewers vs. Dodgers Prediction and Pick
The Brewers were able to maintain their home-field advantage in the first two games of the series, and I think the Dodgers will get a win at home in Game 3.
This is where the Dodgers’ depth really shows. Blake Snell would be the Game 1 or at least Game 2 starter for most teams, but Los Angeles’ acquisition of Tarik Skubal at the trade deadline pushes the veteran southpaw to Game 3 at home.
Robert Gasser has been better than people think for Milwaukee, but I’m not too sure he can go toe-to-toe with Snell. And if the Brewers get a lead, the Brewers would be smart to save their best bullpen arms for the rest of the series.
It is a big price for the Dodgers at -180, though, which is why I’m recommending the run line as my best bet. If you want to just take the moneyline, that’s fine too, but I don’t like giving out best bets at this high of a number.
Pick: Dodgers -1.5 (+129)

item.title: [Reviewing the Brew] Brewers news: Brandon Woodruff update, Shohei Ohtani benching decision, Blake Snell's pre-start comments
item.dc:creator: Owen Jonas
item.description: With a 2-0 series lead over the Los Angeles Dodgers in the National League Championship Series, the Milwaukee Brewers are hoping to win their third consecutive game over the reigning back-to-back World Series champions tonight. The Brewers, who will send Robert Gasser to the mound first in Game 3, are not taking wins in Games 1 and 2 of the NLCS for granted, knowing that the script can quickly be flipped with Dave Roberts' star-studded squad manning the opposing dugout. That said, a 2-0 series l
item.content:encoded:
With a 2-0 series lead over the Los Angeles Dodgers in the National League Championship Series, the Milwaukee Brewers are hoping to win their third consecutive game over the reigning back-to-back World Series champions tonight. The Brewers, who will send Robert Gasser to the mound first in Game 3, are not taking wins in Games 1 and 2 of the NLCS for granted, knowing that the script can quickly be flipped with Dave Roberts' star-studded squad manning the opposing dugout.
That said, a 2-0 series lead in the League Championship Series is uncharted territory for the Brew Crew. The Brewers didn't possess a 2-0 lead in any of their previous four appearances in the LCS -- they were down 0-2 in the ALCS in 1982 before winning three straight, were even at 1-1 through two games in 2011 and 2018, and trailed 0-2 in their NLCS matchup with the Dodgers last year.
While Pat Murphy's squad clearly has the advantage, especially after defeating Los Angeles' dominant starting duo of Tarik Skubal and Yoshinobu Yamamoto, and seeing manager Dave Roberts consider benching 4x MVP Shohei Ohtani, the Brewers remain locked in on winning the series as quickly as possible, knowing that doing so gives them the best chance of eventually securing the first World Series title in franchise history. Staying locked in required them to maintain their focus through yesterday's off-day, during which a trio of intriguing storylines emerged. Let's take a closer look at these three storylines and the implications they could have on the Brewers' path to their first World Series title.
Brandon Woodruff tosses 31-pitch bullpen on Tuesday, narrow chance of returning for potential World Series appearance remains
Perhaps the most exciting piece of news from Tuesday's mid-series off-day was the fact that veteran right-hander Brandon Woodruff kept his hopes of returning for a potential World Series appearance alive by throwing a 31-pitch bullpen. As reported by Curt Hogg of the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel, Woodruff, who reversed course on his decision to have season-ending shoulder surgery and is instead rehabbing his anterior capsule injury, said his stuff felt "pretty good" during his Tuesday afternoon bullpen session.
It remains a long shot that Woodruff returns to the Brewers' pitching staff for a potential World Series appearance, but the franchise legend is certainly doing whatever he can to pitch in the postseason for the first time since 2021. The Brewers not only have to consider whether or not they trust Woodruff to make his return to the mound in the World Series, but also if including him on a potential World Series roster is worth losing an arm who may be more prepared for the Fall Classic.
The best-case scenario is that Woodruff proves he's healthy enough to be included on a potential World Series roster and makes a significant impact on the Brewers' pitching staff down the stretch, but such a scenario feels highly unlikely. That improbability, however, is not stopping Big Woo from putting in the work to be ready for an appearance in the Fall Classic should the Brewers need him.
Dave Roberts says Shohei Ohtani will be in the Game 3 lineup after rumors of Dodgers potentially benching the 4x MVP
Shohei Ohtani has not been his usual dominant self through the Dodgers' first six games of the 2026 postseason. In part due to lingering knee and biceps injuries that caused the 4x MVP to miss time during the regular season, Ohtani has surprisingly been something of an afterthought during Los Angeles' 2026 playoff run.
As a result, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts was reportedly seriously considering benching Ohtani for Game 3 of the NLCS. The consideration was in part due to the fact that rookie southpaw Robert Gasser, who pitches from a low arm slot, is a tough matchup for Ohtani. However, as noted in Roberts' press conference on Tuesday afternoon, Ohtani will be in the Dodgers' starting lineup for Game 3.
Said Roberts, as seen in the video above, Ohtani is "adamant he feels good enough to be in there, he's close to finding something with his swing. And I feel great about it." Whether or not that vote of confidence is genuine or not, Roberts needs his star hitter to find his groove quickly for the Dodgers to slow the momentum of the surging Brewers. Ohtani is just 3-for-20 in the postseason this year, and 1-for-7 with three strikeouts against the Brewers in the NLCS. Whether or not keeping him in the starting lineup is the right decision, Roberts is making the safe call by not removing the generational talent from his NLCS batting order in Game 3.
Dodgers' Game 3 starter Blake Snell comments on change in Brewers' mentality from last year's NLCS
A year ago, Cy Young southpaw Blake Snell took to the podium ahead of his NLCS start against the Brewers and commented on how he wasn't buying the "Average Joes" mindset that Pat Murphy was putting forward. While Snell's comments somewhat missed the mark, due to the fact that the broken financial landscape of baseball will always have the Brewers disadvantaged in comparison to the blank check-bearing Dodgers, it was out of respect that Snell said he didn't believe the Brewers were a bunch of "Average Joes."
This year, the Brewers have shed the underdog mentality, and Snell, who will start Game 3 tonight, has certainly noticed. Said Snell on Tuesday afternoon ahead, "Even the way that Pat [Murphy] talks, and how he talks to the team is way different than last year."
The Brewers are expecting to win this year, which is a stark shift from last year's mentality. No longer does Milwaukee need to do something out of the ordinary to topple the mighty Dodgers and advance to the World Series. Rather, they simply need to play brand of baseball, avoid unforced errors, and continue to prove their roster is capable of success in the postseason. Brewers fans know it, Pat Murphy's squad knows it, and Game 3 starter Blake Snell understands that this isn't the same team who was swept by the Dodgers last year.

item.title: [Reviewing the Brew] Dodgers reportedly considering drastic Shohei Ohtani move after slow start to NLCS rematch with Brewers
item.dc:creator: Owen Jonas
item.description: One year ago, Los Angeles Dodgers superstar Shohei Ohtani essentially single-handedly defeated the Milwaukee Brewers in Game 4 of the National League Championship Series to send his team to the World Series for the second consecutive year. Fast forward 361 days, and Dodgers manager Dave Roberts is considering benching the 4x MVP during his team's NLCS rematch against the Brewers. The report surfaced from Katie Woo and Ken Rosenthal of The Athletic after the Brewers' Game 2 victory over the Dodge
item.content:encoded:
One year ago, Los Angeles Dodgers superstar Shohei Ohtani essentially single-handedly defeated the Milwaukee Brewers in Game 4 of the National League Championship Series to send his team to the World Series for the second consecutive year. Fast forward 361 days, and Dodgers manager Dave Roberts is considering benching the 4x MVP during his team's NLCS rematch against the Brewers.
The report surfaced from Katie Woo and Ken Rosenthal of The Athletic after the Brewers' Game 2 victory over the Dodgers on Monday night, during which Ohtani went 0-for-4 with two strikeouts. According to the duo at The Athletic, Roberts said, "Obviously it hasn’t been good...He doesn’t feel great. I think for me, it’s having a conversation with him tomorrow, kind of try to figure out what’s best for him, what’s best for us."
Ohtani battled a knee injury and right biceps pain throughout the course of the 2026 regular season, and according to his manager, who noted that the superstar "doesn't feel great," those ailments have carried into the postseason. The result has been an uncharacteristically poor performance from Ohtani during the playoffs this year, during which he's collected just three hits -- all singles -- in 20 at-bats and struck out seven times. He does have three walks and a stolen base, but zero RBI and zero extra-base hits in six games is certainly cause for concern for Roberts and his coaching staff.
As a result, there's a very real chance that Ohtani is not in the lineup for Game 3 of the NLCS on Wednesday night. That said, regardless of whether or not the Dodgers' star is actually benched, the turmoil his lack of production has created for Los Angeles' lineup and the resulting difficult decision it has created for Roberts is a distraction that only works in the Brewers' favor.
Dodgers consideration of benching Shohei Ohtani works in Brewers favor regardless of what Dave Roberts decides
Los Angeles is down 0-2 in the series, the Brewers have already beaten their two best starting pitchers in Tarik Skubal and Yoshinobu Yamamoto, and now the Dodgers' manager is asking himself whether or not he should bench a 4x MVP. It's undoubtedly an admirable position to be in for the Brewers -- one that won't be compromised regardless of Roberts' decision on Ohtani.
On one hand, Ohtani certainly isn't right at the plate right now, and faces a tough matchup in Robert Gasser in Game 3. Ohtani struggles with low-slot lefties, and is 0-for-7 with four strikeouts against Gasser in his career. If Roberts elects to keep his struggling, hobbled MVP in the lineup for Game 3 the Brewers certainly have a favorable matchup with Gasser on the bump.
On the other hand, if Roberts elects to replace Ohtani with rookie outfielder Josue De Paula or another bat off the Dodgers' bench, the momentum hit of benching his superstar DH could be significant. The Dodgers' lineup certainly isn't helped when Ohtani is swinging the bat like he has been as of late, but taking him out of the order eliminates the possibility that he will regain his MVP form and come through with a big hit at some point in the series.
It's truly an impossible decision for Roberts, who seldom has to make these types of calls with his star-studded roster. Either he continues to play a clearly hurting Ohtani or he takes a 4x MVP out of the lineup in the NLCS. While he, his coaching staff, and Ohtani himself are mulling over their options, the Brewers, whose attention remains locked in on ending this series as quickly as possible, are the beneficiaries of the turmoil that is occurring in the Dodgers' lineup.

item.title: [Yardbarker] Dodgers Land Brutal Tarik Skubal Prediction Amid NLCS Struggles

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers landed the top pitching prize at the trade deadline by acquiring left-hander Tarik Skubal from the Detroit Tigers, but one early offseason projection suggests their time with the two-time American League Cy Young Award winner could be short-lived.
The Dodgers trail the Milwaukee Brewers 2-0 in the National League Championship Series after losses on Sunday and Monday. Skubal is scheduled to become a free agent once the season ends, and he is expected to command one of the richest contracts in recent Major League Baseball history.
Zachary D. Rymer of Bleacher Report predicts the New York Mets will sign Skubal this winter rather than the Dodgers retaining him.
“The Mets have a good shot at Tarik Skubal simply by virtue of being one of very few teams that can afford him,” Rymer wrote.
ESPN’s Kiley McDaniel surveyed 27 MLB insiders on Skubal’s next deal, and the average projection came out to eight years and $355 million. That average annual value of roughly $44.6 million would top the current record for a pitcher and place the total guarantee among the largest free-agent contracts ever signed.
“When ESPN’s Kiley McDaniel solicited projections for the two-time Cy Young Award winner’s next contract, the average came out to eight years, $355 million. It would be the fourth-largest contract in the history of MLB free agency, and the largest for a full-time pitcher,” Rymer wrote.
“At that rate, the Skubal sweepstakes could come down to which of the Mets, Dodgers or Yankees would be most willing to take the risk. And of those three clubs, the Mets may have the clearest need for a No. 1 starter this winter.”
Only a handful of clubs can realistically meet that price. The Dodgers and New York Yankees both possess deep rotations already, while the Mets have a more obvious hole at the top of their staff after a disappointing 2026 season.
Owner Steve Cohen has shown a willingness to spend at the highest levels, most notably on Juan Soto’s record 15-year, $765 million deal. The Mets also traded Freddy Peralta at the deadline, removing one established option from the rotation and leaving rising right-hander Nolan McLean as a potential co-ace.
Skubal finished the regular season 12-7 with a 2.72 ERA, 186 strikeouts and a 0.96 WHIP across 158 2/3 innings in 26 starts between Detroit and Los Angeles. With the Dodgers specifically, he went 5-2 with a 2.61 ERA and 70 strikeouts in 10 starts covering 62 innings.
He won the American League Cy Young Award in both 2024 and 2025, giving him two consecutive titles as the league’s top pitcher before the midseason trade.
Adding him would give the Mets a clear No. 1 to build around and pair with McLean, though one pitcher alone would not solve every issue on a roster that finished well outside the playoff picture.
The Dodgers still hold significant advantages if they choose to pursue a reunion. They have the financial resources, recent success with back-to-back World Series titles, and remaining frontline options in Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Shohei Ohtani. Losing Skubal would not dismantle their rotation, but retaining him would strengthen their chances of another deep October run.
The offseason market for elite starting pitching is thin outside of Skubal, which should intensify the bidding among the few teams capable of meeting his expected price. Whether the Mets follow through on the predicted pursuit or the Dodgers match any offer remains to be seen once free agency opens.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers landed the biggest fish in the pond at the trade deadline when they acquired left-hander and back-to-back American League Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal from the Detroit Tigers in a blockbuster trade.
However, as they trail the National League Championship Series 2-0, their time with Skubal may be limited. He is a free agent at the end of the season and is widely expected to sign a long-term contract. The Dodgers could certainly pull that off, but he’ll have a lot of suitors in the offseason.
Zachary D. Rymer of Bleacher Report predicts that the Dodgers will lose Skubal to the New York Mets.
“The Mets have a good shot at Tarik Skubal simply by virtue of being one of very few teams that can afford him,” Rymer wrote.
“When ESPN’s Kiley McDaniel solicited projections for the two-time Cy Young Award winner’s next contract, the average came out to eight years, $355 million. It would be the fourth-largest contract in the history of MLB free agency, and the largest for a full-time pitcher.
At that rate, the Skubal sweepstakes could come down to which of the Mets, Dodgers or Yankees would be most willing to take the risk. And of those three clubs, the Mets may have the clearest need for a No. 1 starter this winter.”
Los Angeles Dodgers Predicted to Lose Tarik Skubal
The Dodgers will certainly be in the mix for Skubal when he hits free agency, so they can’t be counted out of the picture, especially with their financial reach. However, that doesn’t mean it’s going to be easy to keep him.
The Mets do like to spend big often, and they have one of the highest payrolls in Major League Baseball. They’ll likely be motivated to make some big moves and get back into the picture in 2027.
But the Dodgers are still fully capable of keeping him around and promising him a chance to compete for a World Series title each year. They have won back-to-back World Series titles after all.
If they do lose Skubal, they’ll still have Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Shohei Ohtani at the top of their rotation, so it wouldn’t be a catastrophic loss.
Still, the Dodgers will want to do whatever they can to try and keep him and take a shot at a championship next year if they lose the NLCS in 2026. They have the money to get it done and will remain a top team if they can keep him.
What Tarik Skubal Would do for New York Mets
Skubal alone won’t fix all the Mets’ problems, but they would at least have an ace to build their pitching staff around and somebody to pair with Nolan McLean at the top of their rotation.
After trading Freddy Peralta, they don’t have that option, so trying for Skubal would make sense and could get them back into contention. But the Dodgers still cannot be counted out simply because they have been able to sign some high-profile free agents in recent years.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] NLCS Overreactions: Dodgers Need to Bench Shohei Ohtani, Will Smith Lost Game 2 and More
item.dc:creator: Noah Camras; Unknown

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are down 0-2 in the National League Championship Series against the Milwaukee Brewers.
After sweeping the Brewers in four games in last year's NLCS, the Dodgers are two wins away from elimination this year.
After losing a tightly-contested Game 1 by a score of 2-1, the Dodgers lost a back-and-forth Game 2 by three runs and suddenly look like they're in serious trouble.
Of course, the series now heads to LA, where the Dodgers will look to hold serve with their home-field advantage, just as the Brewers did.
Thus, it's a major overreaction to say this series is over.
There are some other overreactions that are much more justifiable, though.
Let's look into three of those.
1. The Dodgers Need to Bench Shohei Ohtani
Shohei Ohtani is the best player in baseball. He's a four-time MVP award winner and arguably the scariest player in the batter's box when he's healthy.
That last part is an important caveat, though.
After going 2-for-13 in the NL Division Series, Ohtani is 1-for-7 through two games in the NLCS.
He has just three singles and seven strikeouts thus far in the postseason. His Game 2 performance was another brutal display that included some uncompetitive swings.
So what should the Dodgers do? Should they really bench Ohtani and insert rookie Josue De Paula, who has two walks in three plate appearances thus far this postseason?
It's unlikely LA does that unless Ohtani concedes he's nowhere near 100% and can't play.
What's more likely is the Dodgers keep pushing Ohtani down in the lineup and hope he magically turns things around.
At this point, though, that would appear to be a very optimistic hope.
2. Will Smith Lost the Dodgers NLCS Game 2 — and Potentially More
The Dodgers were confident heading into Games 1 and 2 of the NLCS because they had two of the best pitchers in baseball lined up.
However, Tarik Skubal lasted just five innings in Game 1, and Yoshinobu Yamamoto was chased in the third inning in Game 2.
The Dodgers had to use three relievers in Game 1. They used seven in Game 2.
Yamamoto's night, however, could have looked a lot different with the help of some ABS challenges.
In the first inning, Yamamoto looked like he struck out Brice Turang on three pitches. However, catcher Will Smith didn't challenge a potential strike three, and on the sixth pitch of the at-bat, Turang doubled (and ended up scoring).
In the bottom of the third inning, Yamamoto again looked like he struck out Turang. The sixth pitch of the at-bat, which came on a 3-2 count, appeared to clip the edge of the zone. Yamamoto even went to tap his head to signal Smith to challenge, but the catcher chose not to.
That would've been the second out of the inning, and William Contreras flied out as the next batter. Instead, the inning was extended, and Jake Bauers drew a 12-pitch walk after Contreras' fly out before Christian Yelich hit a two-run single, chasing Yamamoto from the game.
Smith, of course, wouldn't have had to challenge if the home plate umpire made the correct call. But these two moments — more so the second one — seemingly would have called for a challenge, especially with Yamamoto asking for it the second time.
Things would have been much different with a challenge, and LA still could have lost the game. But it feels as if Yamamoto could have pitched longer had those challenges been called — and thus, LA wouldn't have had to use eight pitchers and tax their bullpen in Game 2 even if they lost.
3. The Brewers Bullpen is Too Dominant for the Dodgers Offense
The Brewers had the best bullpen in the National League throughout the regular season. They've taken their game to the next level in the postseason.
After allowing just one earned run across 19 innings in the NL Division Series against the San Diego Padres, the Brewers bullpen has pitched 9.2 scoreless innings in the NLCS against the Dodgers.
In Game 2, they made history, becoming the first relief corps to ever have five perfect innings in a postseason game.
The Dodgers offense struggled mightily in the NLDS, going just 1-for-18 with runners in scoring position.
Thus far in the NLCS, they're 1-for-10.
Ohtani is struggling. Smith is struggling. The Dodgers offense mustered just three hits in Game 2.
Now, the Brewers bullpen will be rested heading into Game 3 on Wednesday in LA. If the offense doesn't wake up, things could get ugly — and fast — for the Dodgers.

Noah Camras graduated from the University of Southern California in 2022 with a B.A. in Journalism and a minor in sports media studies. He was born and raised in Los Angeles and has extensively covered Southern California sports in his career. Noah is the publisher of Dodgers on SI after contributing as a writer and editor over the last three years.

item.title: [New York Post] Dodgers’ biggest advantages are disappearing at the worst possible time

item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE – One by one, their advantages are vanishing.
Their edge in starting pitching?
Marginalized by the Brewers’ lineup.
Their superior offensive firepower?
Held without a home run in the first two games of this National League Championship Series.
Shohei Ohtani?
Reduced to being blown away by mid-90s fastballs.
The Dodgers are behind by two games in this race to four wins, and in the wake of their 7-4 defeat in Game 2 at American Family Field, they have to be praying for the Brewers to run out of gas before they reach the finish line.
“It’s certainly a challenge,” manager Dave Roberts said.
Before the Dodgers can win this series, they will have to get back into it first. They will play at home over the next three games. They have Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow lined up to pitch in Games 3 and 4, respectively.
“Still a pretty good scenario we’re in,” first baseman Freddie Freeman said.
Sending Snell and Glasnow to the mound won’t mean anything, however, if the Dodgers don’t start hitting. An error or wild pitch by the Brewers played a role in every run scored by the Dodgers, who collected only three hits, all of them coming against starter Logan Henderson. The four relievers deployed by Brewers manager Pat Murphy combined to pitch five no-hit innings.
The Dodgers will have to jumpstart their offense with a version of Shohei Ohtani who remains physically diminished.
Ohtani was 0 for 4 in Game 2, failing to reach base in a game for the first time this postseason. Pitching as if they didn’t think that Ohtani couldn’t hurt them, the Brewers attacked the four-time Most Valuable Player, leading to a couple of strikeouts in which he looked completely overmatched.
Henderson struck him out with three fastballs in the first inning. Left-hander Jojo Romero tricked him into waving at a sweeper that ended up in the batter’s box on the other side of home plate in the fifth.
Ohtani is batting .150 in the playoffs without a single run batted in. He’s struck out seven times in 20 at-bats. His last home run was on Aug. 18.
“It’s hard to see,” Betts said. “We know he’s working and hopefully he gets out of it. We need him. We need him for sure.”
Ohtani alone couldn’t take down the Brewers, regardless how well he was playing. In addition to a relentless bullpen, they have an unspectacular but industrious offense. They have the kind of edge that makes it obvious they believe they can take down the two-time defending World Series champions.
Game 2 was a prime example of that. If there was a game the Brewers were expected to drop, it was this one. Yoshinobu Yamamoto was pitching for the Dodgers.
The Brewers didn’t just beat Yamamoto. They wore him down, pushed him out of the game after only 2 ⅔ innings and forced Roberts to empty his bullpen. Tarik Skubal lasted only five innings against them in Game 1.
The result was an unmitigated disaster for the Dodgers, who have made it an annual tradition to have the Japanese right-hander bail them out of trouble at this time of the year.
The Dodgers were intimately familiar with the script from which the Brewers read.
Run up the pitch count of the starter.
Force him out of the game early.
Get into the other team’s bullpen.
Only this time, the Dodgers weren’t the team executing the game plan. They were the team against which the plan was being executed, and Yamamoto was the target of the attack.
Once the game morphed into a battle of the bullpens, the game was decided. The Brewers were able to play to their greatest strength. The Dodgers had to expose their greatest weakness.
To win the World Series last year, the Dodgers had to overcome a three-games-to-two deficit against the Toronto Blue Jays. Their title run the previous year started with them reversing a two-games-to-one deficit against the San Diego Padres.
The Dodgers have overcome deficits before.
But the Brewers are presenting them with the sort of problems they might not even be able to solve.

item.title: [True Blue LA] Dodgers need Brewers help to score, can’t stop William Contreras in NLCS Game 2 loss
item.dc:creator: Eric Stephen

In a game with four lead changes and two ties, the Dodgers couldn’t get a big hit to save their life, while William Contreras had three different run-scoring hits in the Brewers’ 7-4 win at American Family Field on Monday afternoon in Milwaukee.
