item.content:encoded:
Despite an injury-plagued season for Shohei Ohtani, 2026 has been a really good year for the Los Angeles Dodgers. After signing Kyle Tucker in the offseason and trading for Tarik Skubal at the trade deadline, they loaded up their roster yet again en route to the second best record in all of baseball. But with the Dodgers painted as the “bad guy” over the last few seasons, the team may ultimately have a major say in the potential 2027 lockout.
With a total luxury tax payroll of over $420 million, the Dodgers spent more money than the four lowest-spending in the league combined. Not only has that drawn the ire from opposing fan bases, but it puts the Dodgers into the spotlight regarding the Major League Baseball Collective Bargaining Agreement negotiations. The owners are eyeing a salary cap to curb spending. But that’s a concept that players like Kiké Hernández refuse to entertain.
As reported by Andy McCullough of The Athletic, the Dodgers clubhouse has not been immune to feeling the burn of that ire and the pressure of a potential lockout next season. But that doesn’t mean that the players are getting desperate. Hernández even acknowledged that the guys in the Dodgers clubhouse know exactly how the game is played on and off the field.
“Whenever things like a CBA come around, there always has to be a bad guy in order for the opposition to want to change things,” Hernández told The Athletic. “And we just happen to be the ones to blame, at this point. Obviously, probably well-deserved, because of the way the last couple of years have gone. Especially with the spending.”
Obviously that spending has paid off for the Dodgers, but does it put them at an unfair competitive advantage?
Kiké Hernández feels like the Dodgers are doing things the right way
Outside of the COVID-shortened season in 2020, the Dodgers have not had a payroll under $200 million since 2018. But as we’ve seen with teams like the New York Mets, spending money doesn’t always equate to a World Series title, or even fielding winning teams that can make it to the postseason.
But with the opportunity to win their third consecutive World Series and their fourth in seven seasons, the Dodgers have spent their money the right way. They’ve made the majority of their acquisitions count and they haven’t taken on too many bad contracts in recent years. The team even boasts a strong minor league system with affordable players like Josue De Paula.
Granted, the deferred money with Ohtani’s contract is the mother of all workarounds, but they still played by the rules when finalizing that deal. That is something that Hernández feels like every team should be doing.
“If you own a team, it would make sense that you’re trying to make that team the best possible, in order to win,” added Hernández. “Because if not, you’re just treating the team as a stock. And why would you want to compete against other people if you’re just trying to make money? Sell the team to somebody who actually wants to compete and win.”
Obviously professional sports are a business. A multi-billion dollar business at that. But at the heart of that business is a game. As Hernández describes it, the Dodgers are just out to win that game and collect another ring. Other teams may lack the budget to stretch their payroll like the Dodgers, but who is most to blame for that?
As of this season, there are just two MLB owners who don’t have a net worth of at least a billion dollars. Bob Castellini of the Cincinnati Reds has $400 million to his name and Dick Monfort Colorado Rockies has a net worth of $700 million. So there is plenty of money to go around baseball. It just comes down to who is willing to spend it in order to win. And winning is something that the players don’t want to negotiate on.

item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX -- The two-time defending World Series champions are in a rare funk.
The Los Angeles Dodgers lost their season-high seventh game in a row in a stunning collapse Friday night after the Arizona Diamondbacks rallied for a 4-3 win when rookie Ryan Waldschmidt hit a two-run, walk-off homer against closer Edwin Diaz.
"A loss is a loss, but to get walked off never feels good," Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. "We didn't play a clean game, a great game, on either side of the baseball, but we did enough to put ourselves in position to win a game.
"Unfortunately, we couldn't finish it."
It was another rough outing for Diaz, who has an 11.00 ERA over 11 outings this season. The 32-year-old is a three-time All-Star, but he hasn't helped the Dodgers much after signing a three-year, $69 million deal during the offseason.
Waldschmidt connected on Diaz's hanging slider, hitting it into the left-center field seats for his second career homer and first big league walk-off.
"It's the slider," Diaz said. "The fastball was great today, but I missed the slider right in the middle. I think I was trying to be perfect with the pitch, and I'm missing right in the middle. I've got to be better. I'm a big league pitcher, so I've got to make pitches."
The Dodgers were swept by the Boston Red Sox and Chicago Cubs coming into Friday night's game. They still have a comfortable lead in the National League West -- 7 games in front of the Diamondbacks -- despite a 10-16 record since July 5.
Roberts acknowledged that Diaz has been struggling since his return from the injured list on July 29, but the manager wasn't necessarily ready to try a new closer. His reasoning was simple: There's no clear-cut alternative.
"Honestly, you've got to look at the options," Roberts said. "The way some of these guys are throwing, they're not throwing great either."
The Dodgers still look like a formidable team, particularly after adding ace left-hander Tarik Skubal in a trade-deadline deal with the Detroit Tigers last week. Two-time Cy Young Award winner Blake Snell is slated to return Tuesday after missing most of the season because of injuries.
And the lineup still has plenty of star power with Shohei Ohtani, Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts and Kyle Tucker.
Roberts said before Friday's game that the remedy for the recent troubles was simple.
"We've just got to play better," Roberts said. "I don't think the standings -- I mean they're important, they matter -- but I just feel like with the talent we have, we've just got to play good baseball and it'll take care of itself. It always does."br/]

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Blake Snell’s rocky outing leads to de facto bullpen game

item.content:encoded:
The Dodgers needed one win to send the Atlanta Braves to the brink of elimination on Sunday. Instead, the Braves lineup forced an early exit from Blake Snell and scored two defining runs against the bullpen in a 3-2 win over the Dodgers, forcing the series back to Atlanta for Games 3 and 4.
It wasn't the first rocky outing for Snell against Atlanta this season, as he only managed to toss three innings while allowing four runs in his 2026 debut back on May 8 before being placed on the injured list. The southpaw had looked like his usual dominant stretch once he returned in August, but the ultimate test was to see how he would perform against the lone team that roughed him up.
Snell made quick work of Drake Baldwin for the first out, but after allowing a one-out single to Ronald Acuña Jr., he walked both Matt Olson and Ozzie Albies to load the bases. Snell managed to get Michael Harris II to fly out in foul territory for a crucial second out, but Mauricio Dubón tacked on the game's first run with an infield single. Snell faced seven hitters in the first inning, needing 27 pitches to give the Dodgers a chance to hit.
Snell's biggest flaw on Sunday was his inability to get quick innings, unlike Tarik Skubal on Saturday. Snell needed four pitches to get two quick outs in the second inning, but allowed a six-pitch walk to Baldwin and needed another eight to strike out Acuña. Snell allowed another two-out baserunner in the third inning, this time a single from Harris, needing 19 pitches after tossing 18 the inning prior.
Snell's hopes at a clean inning were dashed in the fourth inning, as he walked a pair of hitters and tossed 26 pitches before the plug was pulled on his night. The Dodgers got him off the hook in the bottom of the fourth inning with a Freddie Freeman home run, but the Dodgers employed six relievers out of the bullpen over their final 5 1/3 innings on the mound.
Snell had a postseason to remember last year, as his defining moment came in Game 1 of the NLCS against the Milwaukee Brewers, facing the minimum over eight shutout innings. Sunday's outing was the first time he failed to log four innings in a postseason start since he began the 2022 Wild Card series against the New York Mets back when he was a San Diego Padre. Out of the 90 pitches he tossed against Atlanta, 47 of them went for strikes.
Snell's final start of the regular season was limited to just one inning after he dealt with left groin inflammation. Dave Roberts was quick to deny any concern over Snell's groin issue, noting that he was battling himself on the mound.
"No, it wasn't that. He was fighting himself in his delivery all game. Today, I just think the fastball was really good, the changeup was good at times, but I think, in total, didn't have fastball command, didn't have slider command, and the changeup wasn't there. He was pulling it. I think overall it wasn't the groin, and he wasn't sharp tonight."
Roberts felt optimistic about his chances of Snell on the mound while Atlanta went with their own bullpen game, beginning with left-hander Ray Kerr. The pieces just couldn't fall into place on Sunday.
"Felt great. Anytime I feel I have Blake Snell lined up against any pitcher felt good. Going to getting Kerr out of the game and then getting [Grant] Holmes out of the game, I felt really good where we were at. I really did. We just couldn't execute as the game progressed."
Now the Dodgers will face the only pitcher to shut them out in the regular season, left-hander Chris Sale, in a crucial Game 3 at Truist Park on Tuesday. Yoshinobu Yamamoto will take the mound for the first time in the playoffs since his Herculean performance in Game 7 of the 2025 World Series.

item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers left-handed pitcher Tarik Skubal will kick off Game 1 of the National League Division Series against the Atlanta Braves on Saturday.
The Dodgers are yet to name their starters for the rest of the series, but Blake Snell and Yoshinobu Yamamoto are expected to pitch the next two games.
On Saturday morning, the Dodgers will announce their official 26-man roster for the NLDS.
On Friday, manager Dave Roberts provided a hint as to how many pitchers and position players will make up the squad.
“I do know we're going to go with 14 [position players] and 12 [pitchers], and now trying to figure out the bench bat, who are the extra players, is it going to be a pinch runner," Roberts said. "Yeah, I think that's kind of where we're at, and then finalizing the last reliever is always front of mind.”
In other news, the team at Dodgers On SI provided some expert predictions as to how the series will shake out. Atlanta had 94 regular season wins and is riding high after beating the Philadelphia Phillies in Game 3 of the wild-card round on Thursday, but the Dodgers have had five days of rest and are looking to make history this October.
Finally, superstar Shohei Ohtani broke his silence amid his recent activation from the injured list just in time to play in the final five regular season games of 2026. The four-time MVP isn't sure what is causing his nagging knee and biceps injuries, but is confident that he will manage it while he and his team do their best to collect 11 more wins.
“I haven't been able to get a good grasp of the root cause of all this," Ohtani said. "I think that process is going to happen during the offseason when I'm going to have a little bit more time to be able to address it. But as of now, it's something I'm just going to have to manage."

item.content:encoded:
Por problemas de lesión
Shohei Ohtani sigue siendo cuestionante para los Dodgers
**Ohtani llega a los playoffs con molestias y Dodgers abren ante Braves**
LOS ÁNGELES.— Shohei Ohtani llega a la postemporada todavía tratando de convivir con las molestias que lo alejaron del montículo después del Juego de Estrellas y que lo llevaron por primera vez a la lista de lesionados de los Dodgers de Los Ángeles.
El japonés no tiene claro todavía el origen de las molestias en el bíceps derecho, la rodilla izquierda y el cuello, situación que deberá ser evaluada con mayor profundidad durante la temporada muerta.
“Hasta ahora no he podido comprender bien la causa fundamental de todo esto, así que creo que ese proceso tendrá lugar durante la temporada baja, cuando tenga un poco más de tiempo para abordarlo. Por ahora, es algo que simplemente tendré que manejar”, explicó Ohtani el viernes a través de un intérprete.
El estelar jugador de dos vías regresó de la lista de lesionados cuando restaban apenas cinco partidos de la serie regular y bateó de 21-5, con ocho ponches, una base por bolas y un doble.
Ohtani, sin embargo, aseguró que se siente mejor y que su swing está recuperando su ritmo.
“Mi cuerpo se siente muy bien en general. Siento que mi swing está en un mejor lugar, se siente fluido. Solo algunos pequeños ajustes aquí y allá y estaré listo”, manifestó.
Los Dodgers comenzarán este sábado la Serie Divisional de la Liga Nacional contra los Bravos de Atlanta, en el primer paso en busca de su tercer campeonato consecutivo de la Serie Mundial.
El dirigente Dave Roberts no quiso adelantar qué versión de Ohtani podrá ofrecer en la postemporada, aunque confía en que pueda responder cuando llegue el momento.
“Espero cosas buenas. Realmente lo hago. Simplemente no lo hemos visto lo suficiente como para pronosticarlo”, señaló Roberts.
### Braves llegan con rotación golpeada
Mientras los Dodgers han tenido cinco días para descansar y preparar la Serie Divisional, Atlanta llega a Los Ángeles después de eliminar a los Filis de Filadelfia en tres partidos de la Serie de Comodines.
La situación de su rotación es uno de los principales temas antes del inicio de la serie.
Chris Sale, su as, lanzó los últimos cuatro outs del tercer partido ante Filadelfia con apenas un día de descanso. Había realizado 95 lanzamientos en el primer encuentro de esa serie, por lo que todavía no está definido si podrá abrir el segundo partido ante los Dodgers.
Además, los Bravos descartaron para esta serie a los abridores Martín Pérez, por molestias en la espalda, y Bryce Elder, por un problema en la rodilla.
El dirigente Walt Weiss reconoció que el bullpen podría asumir una carga importante, especialmente durante los primeros partidos.
“Hay una posibilidad de que tengamos que lanzar muchas entradas con nuestro bullpen, especialmente en los primeros dos partidos”, dijo Weiss.
### El calor también juega
A la exigencia del playoff se suma el intenso calor que afecta a Los Ángeles.
Para el primer partido, programado para la tarde del sábado, se pronostica una temperatura máxima de 100 grados Fahrenheit, unos 38 grados Celsius, muy por encima del promedio de 81 grados para esta época del año.
El domingo tampoco habrá mucho alivio, con una temperatura proyectada de 99 grados Fahrenheit.
Tarik Skubal será el abridor de los Dodgers en el primer partido, mientras que los lanzadores de ambos equipos deberán lidiar con unas condiciones poco habituales para un partido de octubre.
El récord de temperatura durante un partido en el Dodger Stadium es de 103 grados Fahrenheit, registrado en dos ocasiones: durante el primer partido de la Serie Mundial de 2017 contra Houston y en un encuentro de temporada regular ante Cleveland en 2024.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Mets are in offseason mode and are lacking a true ace to anchor their starting rotation. Nonetheless, one potential guy could fill that need: Los Angeles Dodgers starter Tarik Skubal.
While New York can spend the money under owner Steve Cohen, the question is whether he and Mets president of baseball operations David Stearns want to commit to the long-term contract and money Skubal will demand.
Although the Mets need an ace, Underscore Media's Sal Licata believes that New York should stay away from Skubal, given that the team will still have significant holes on the roster.
"In this particular spot, do you think Tarik Skubal alone is the difference-maker for the Mets? I don't," Licata said in an Oct. 1 Underscore Media video on X. "I think they need more than one guy atop their rotation, and if you're telling me that there are going to be at least some kind of limitations, and forget the collective bargaining agreement, all that stuff, if there is going to be some kind of limitations.
"There always are; even Steve Cohen has his limit. It's stupid to have the luxury tax threshold and not be able to go out and balance the team out if you need to. You don't want to just go all in on three freaking players. It just doesn't work."
Mets Urged to Follow Yankees Path
Moreover, Licata believes the Mets should take the approach the New York Yankees did when they didn't re-sign Juan Soto and opted to spread that money around rather than pay one guy.
"If that's going to be a thing, then why wouldn't you rather spread that out a little bit?" Licata added. "In theory, do what the Yankees did after they lost out on Soto and spread it out a little bit and allow you to add multiple pieces."
Tarik Skubal Could Pitch in Major Market Like New York
Meanwhile, SNY's Keith Raad says that if the Mets do make a serious run at Skubal in free agency, they wouldn't have to worry about the veteran ace having that shock of pitching in a big market. Skubal spent most of his career with the Detroit Tigers, but his midseason trade to the Dodgers shows he can perform for a team in a big market and with expectations.
"Skubal has been there and done that a little bit, even though he's pitched in Detroit and the fact that he's pitching well for the Dodgers as the guy in the trade shows me that he would be fine," Raad said in an Oct. 1 appearance on SNY.
"The only cautionary tale I would have is, again, Mets in-house; they brought in people, they brought in players that maybe started to go south. They have not been able to get them right. That's the part that the Mets need to figure out in player acquisition. Can we get them back to the back of the baseball card, just a simple average of who they are?"
Since the trade to the Dodgers, Skubal is 5-2 with a 2.61 ERA and 70 strikeouts in 10 appearances, per StatMuse.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Mets Issued Clear Free Agency Message on Dodgers' Tarik Skubal appeared first on HEAVY.

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — With less than 24 hours before the first pitch of Game 1 of the NLDS, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts made his decision: Tarik Skubal will take the ball Saturday afternoon against the Braves.
The choice came from a rotation that gives the Dodgers perhaps as much depth as any team could ask for. Skubal earned the assignment over reigning World Series MVP Yoshinobu Yamamoto, fellow two-time Cy Young Award winner Blake Snell and All-Star right-hander Tyler Glasnow.
“With the four guys, it doesn't really matter who, but I think that we feel good about Tarik taking the baseball tomorrow afternoon,” Roberts said.
As it turns out, Skubal knew his assignment before the regular season was even over.
When Roberts pulled him after just 75 pitches in his final start in San Francisco, Skubal initially wondered why. He approached his manager, expecting there might be another reason for the early exit.
Instead, Roberts gave him a message that changed the rest of his week.
“He came and shook my hand. I was at kind of a low pitch count, I thought in the moment I was going to be able to finish the game. And he was like, ‘Get ready for Game 1,’” Skubal said.
Skubal said he was “obviously excited and fired up and ready to go.”
Now comes a new experience for the reigning back-to-back unanimous Cy Young winner.
For everything Skubal has accomplished, he has never had the opportunity to pitch at home in October. That changes Saturday, when he takes the mound in front of a Dodgers crowd for the opening game of the NLDS.
“I’m excited for the opportunity to throw in front of the fans,” Skubal said.
The left-hander also knows exactly what the atmosphere can feel like when he pitched for the Tigers.
“Usually when I walk out onto the field in a playoff game, it's usually received with a lot of boos,” Skubal said. “So I'm excited to get some cheers in there for us. And to pitch at home, I think it's going to be a ton of fun in front of this atmosphere.”
His approach for the biggest start of his Dodgers career?
Keep it simple.
“I have to be really good at what makes me good,” Skubal said.
The weather will provide another challenge, with triple-digit temperatures expected Saturday. Skubal, however, doesn't appear particularly concerned.
“We probably won't have to go to the bathroom. Just sweat it out,” he joked.
The extra time between starts has also been welcomed by the left-hander.
“I think for a starter, it's easiest to take time off,” Skubal said.
He also credited Dodgers fans for the reception he has received since arriving in Los Angeles and said he is looking forward to finally pitching in front of them in October.
“I’m excited to throw in front of them tomorrow.”
Ohtani Says His Swing Is Trending in the Right Direction
While Skubal prepares for his first postseason start at Dodger Stadium, Shohei Ohtani is preparing to return to October action after recently being activated from the 15-day injured list.
Ohtani said he feels really good overall and believes his swing has benefited from the extended break.
“I do feel like my swing is in a better place,” Ohtani said. “Just little tweaks here and there, and I’ll be ready for tomorrow.”
The time away from games, he said, has given him an opportunity to make adjustments while managing the ailments that surfaced during the second half.
“Being on the IL has taught me a lot,” Ohtani said.
But the Dodgers' star acknowledged that his lingering biceps and knee issues remain something he will have to manage throughout the postseason.
Asked whether those injuries could require attention during the offseason, Ohtani said he has not yet identified the root cause of everything he has been dealing with.
“I haven't been able to get a good grasp of the root cause of all this,” Ohtani said. “I think that process is going to happen during the off-season when I'm going to have a little bit more time to be able to address it. But as of now, it's something I'm just going to have to manage.”
That reality isn't unique to Ohtani.
Roberts said most of the players currently preparing for the postseason are dealing with some level of physical issue.
“Most players that are performing now are not at 100%,” Roberts said.
Still, Roberts expects Ohtani to perform well when the Dodgers open their series Saturday. He also expressed confidence in Freddie Freeman, whose own lingering injuries have been a storyline heading into October, particularly after seeing Freeman in Thursday's intrasquad game.
The Dodgers will enter the NLDS with a roster expected to feature 14 position players and 12 pitchers, according to Roberts. He was not yet ready to announce the starters for Games 2 and 3.
For now, the focus belongs to Skubal.
The Dodgers acquired him to pitch in moments exactly like this one. On Saturday, in front of a home crowd and with the season entering its most important stretch, he gets the opportunity to show what he can do.
And unlike his previous playoff outings in opposing ballparks, this time, the cheers will be for him.

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA—Tomorrow marks the start of the Los Angeles Dodgers’ quest for a third consecutive World Series championship, beginning with a rematch against the Atlanta Braves in the 2026 National League Division Series.
Today, both clubs hold their final workout before Saturday’s scorching mid-day opener, and we’ve got plenty of new updates and clarity on the Dodgers’ plans for the two games this weekend.
Dodgers’ NLDS Rotation Comes Into Focus With Skubal Tabbed for Game One
Leading up to the postseason, many asked what order the Dodgers would put on their star-studded starting rotation, and now we have part of an answer: two-time AL Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal will start Game One of the NLDS against the Braves on Saturday.
That was a shock to many, especially since 2025 World Series MVP Yoshinobu Yamamoto was considered the clear-cut favorite to lead the charge in the postseason.
The move also isn’t entirely based on the Braves’ struggles versus left-handed pitching this season; Skubal on Friday confirmed that he learned of his Game One start way back during his last outing in San Francisco, where he tossed seven shutout innings to close his 2026 regular season.
While Dave Roberts was less revealing about his outlook for Games Two and Three of the NLDS, he admitted the team would have a decision by the end of Friday’s workout, but the stars are starting to align themselves on what the likely order will be.
Yamamoto, who faced hitters on Wednesday, is now lined up to start on regular rest against the Braves during Game Three, as reported by Taro Abe of Japan’s Chunichi Sports.
That would place left-hander Blake Snell for Game Two, after Skubal and before Yamamoto and Tyler Glasnow, who threw a simulated game on Thursday for a possible Game Four if needed.
There were really no “wrong” answers for Dave Roberts and the Dodgers, but this allows them to focus on the Braves’ left-handed disadvantage and decide whether to go for the series sweep or swing with their best starter, Yamamoto, on the mound in Game Three, where he’ll likely go toe-to-toe with Chris Sale.
Dodgers Look to Exploit Braves’ Left-Handed Weakness With Southpaw-Heavy Staff
After tabbed left-hander Tarik Skubal with the ball in Game One of the NLDS, it starts a running theme for the Dodgers’ plan against the Braves, and that is their inability and struggles to hit left-handed pitching.
The Braves posted just a 91 wRC+ against southpaws during the regular season, tied for 24th in MLB. They also ranked 21st in wOBA (.306), 28th in OBP (.300), and tied for 16th in batting average (.240), while their 7.0% walk rate against lefties ranked 29th.
That combination gives the Dodgers plenty of reason to load up on southpaws in the NLDS, particularly with Tarik Skubal and Blake Snell available. Skubal is already set to start Game One, giving Los Angeles a lefty right out of the gate.
Atlanta’s overall offense was productive enough to win 94 games, but its struggles against lefties provide the Dodgers with a specific weakness to attack throughout the series.
While the Dodgers have yet to announce a Game Two starter, all signs point to fellow left-hander Blake Snell, with Yoshinobu Yamamoto to follow him in Game Three at Atlanta.
As far as the Dodgers’ bullpen construction, depending on what split they have on the 26-man roster, they have plenty of left-handed options to choose from, including deadline acquisition Kris Bubic.
Dodgers manager Dave Roberts confirmed Friday that the team would go with a 14-12 split for their 26-man roster, and with four starting pitchers, that leaves eight spots for the bullpen, with left-handers Tanner Scott, Jack Dreyer and Alex Vesia locked for that role.
Chris Sale Likely Out of Games One and Two as Dodgers Avoid Atlanta’s Ace Early
In an effort to push the Braves past the Phillies for their first postseason series win since the 2021 season, Chris Sale came in on two days of rest out of the bullpen to collect the final four outs of Game Three.
Despite the Braves leading 6-2 and their closer, Raisel Iglesias, available in the bullpen, new Braves skipper Walt Weiss opted for the kill shot by bringing in his best pitcher, Chris Sale.
That move, however important it was for that particular game, has changed the landscape of the Braves’ pitching plan for the NLDS, as Sale is not lined up to pitch Game One and now may not be in play for Game Two on Sunday either.
“We’re gonna err on the side of giving him (time to rest) if it’s even close… A lot of it’s going to depend on how Chris feels… Certainly don’t want to jeopardize him and his health. He just happened to feel great yesterday when he got to the park, and that’s why he was in play.”
While this could simply be Walt Weiss playing a little October gamesmanship, keeping Chris Sale away from Games One and Two would certainly give Atlanta a chance to catch the Dodgers off guard, though Dave Roberts has plenty of postseason experience himself.
Of course, Weiss could also be telling the truth. If Atlanta really plans to save Sale for his return to Truist Park, the Braves’ decision to use him in relief during Game Three of the Wild Card Series becomes even more curious.
The Braves are already down two starters in left-hander Martín Pérez and right-hander Bryce Elder, with Weiss confirming that both will not be on the NLDS roster but possibly on the NLCS roster if Atlanta advances.
That leaves the Braves with a trio of Chris Sale (down until Game Three), Tyler Mahle, and Grant Holmes, who has been used in relief as a bulk inning guy from the bullpen.
The Braves are likely to launch a bullpen game for Game One in Los Angeles on Saturday, with Mahle set to start Game Two on normal rest after a masterful outing tossing seven innings of one-run ball.
Still, the likelihood of the Dodgers seeing Sale only once this series, and as late as Game Three, is a massive advantage for Dave Roberts and Co.
Dodgers vs. Braves: How the 2026 Head-to-Head Series Shook Out
The Dodgers didn’t exactly dominate their head-to-head matchup with the Braves this season. Los Angeles went just 1-5 against Atlanta in six regular-season meetings, getting outscored 26-15 in the process.
The teams first met at Dodger Stadium from May 8th-10th, with the Dodgers taking the opener 3-1 before Atlanta won the next two games by identical 7-2 scores. The Braves then delivered an even bigger blow in the final regular-season series, sweeping Los Angeles at Truist Park from August 25th-27th. Atlanta won the opener by one run, walked off in the middle game, and finished the sweep with a 1-0 Chris Sale shutout.
This matchup also comes with some unfinished postseason business. The Dodgers and Braves last met in the 2021 NLCS, when Atlanta knocked Los Angeles out in six games before winning the World Series. The Dodgers battled back from a 2-0 series deficit to cut the deficit to one game, but the Braves slammed the door in Game Six at Truist Park.
Five years later, the two teams meet again with another trip to the NLCS on the line. After Atlanta owned the regular-season matchup, the Dodgers now have a chance to change the story when the NLDS opens Saturday at Dodger Stadium.

item.content:encoded:
Yoshinobu Yamamoto became a Los Angeles Dodgers legend in the 2025 World Series. But he won't be the first pitcher the team trots out in this year's National League Division Series.
Instead, it will be trade deadline acquisition Tarik Skubal starting Game 1 against the Atlanta Braves on Saturday, the team announced Friday.
The Dodgers' postseason rotation consists of Skubal, Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow, a high-priced and high-performing quartet, all with postseason experience. Yamamoto, Snell and Glasnow were all key parts of last year's championship team, including relief appearances in Game 7 of the World Series.
Skubal, meanwhile, has a 2.04 ERA and 56 strikeouts in six career postseason starts, all in the wild-card and division rounds. The Detroit Tigers went 3-3 with him on the mound, though he only had one truly bad start in Game 5 of the 2024 ALDS against the Cleveland Guardians.
Platoon splits could have swung the decision as much as anything, as the Braves rank 11th in MLB with a .730 OPS against right-handed pitchers, like Yamamoto, compared to 21st at .696 against left-handers.
The starting decisions for Games 1 and 2 also matter quite a bit in a division series, as they also decide which pitchers are available for later in the series. Assuming the Dodgers stick to their rotation quartet, they'd go into an all-hands-on-deck Game 5 with Skubal starting and Yamamoto possibly working behind him in relief on short rest.
Both Skubal and Yamamoto were excellent in this year's regular season, with Yamamoto the only pitcher to last the entire year in the Dodgers' rotation.
Skubal, acquired at the deadline in exchange for prospects Zyhir Hope, River Ryan and Brady Smith, missed a month earlier this year with loose bodies in his pitching elbow but holds a 2.61 ERA with the Dodgers. No pitcher in MLB had more fWAR than him following the deadline.

item.title: [Field Level Media] Dodgers not talking 3-peat yet as Braves enter NLDS with confidence
item.description: LOS ANGELES — The potential road to history for the Los Angeles Dodgers begins with a reunion as the National League Division Series starts Saturday afternoon with a visit from the Atlanta Braves. Freddie Freeman has been a major postseason contributor during the Dodgers’ consecutive World Series titles, and the veteran will be in the heart of the order again in a matchup against his former team. Freeman also was invaluable in the 2021 World Series when the Braves won their most recent title. Fr
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — The potential road to history for the Los Angeles Dodgers begins with a reunion as the National League Division Series starts Saturday afternoon with a visit from the Atlanta Braves.
Freddie Freeman has been a major postseason contributor during the Dodgers’ consecutive World Series titles, and the veteran will be in the heart of the order again in a matchup against his former team.
Freeman also was invaluable in the 2021 World Series when the Braves won their most recent title. Freeman joined the Dodgers as a free agent in 2022 after Atlanta moved on to Matt Olson as their first baseman.
While Freeman has won three rings in five seasons, the Dodgers are trying to become the first National League club to win championships in three consecutive years. Only two American League franchises have ever done it: the New York Yankees and Oakland Athletics.
The Yankees were the last to accomplish the feat when they won championships in 1998, 1999 and 2000.
“We don’t need to be adding any extra pressure onto ourselves,” Dodgers third baseman Max Muncy said. “We’ve been saying that for a long time. When you talk about three-peating, you’re putting that extra pressure on it that doesn’t need to be there. Winning a World Series is already hard enough as it is.”
After returning from a biceps injury during the final week of the regular season, Shohei Ohtani will be back atop the Los Angeles order when the club’s postseason run begins.
Left-hander Tarik Skubal was named the Dodgers’ Game 1 starter over right-hander Yoshinobu Yamamoto. Skubal arrived just before the trade deadline in a deal with the Detroit Tigers and went 5-2 with a 2.61 ERA in 10 starts for his new club.
Skubal is 0-1 with a 4.91 ERA in two career starts against Atlanta, including an outing in April when he gave up two runs over seven innings in a no-decision.
The Braves opened their postseason by getting past the Philadelphia Phillies in the wild-card round. Atlanta won a winner-take-all Game 3 on Thursday behind a three-run home run from Michael Harris II and a dominating day on the mound. Six pitchers kept Philadelphia in check, including staff ace Chris Sale, who recorded the final four outs.
The Braves face the Dodgers after going 5-1 against them in the regular season, including a three-game home sweep in late August.
“Everyone knows the Dodgers have a juggernaut, but we played well against them this year,” Atlanta manager Walt Weiss said. “I know that doesn’t carry a whole lot of stock. Once the playoffs begin, everybody starts at zero. The Dodgers are healthier now than they were when we saw them.”
Weiss has yet to name his Game 1 starter, with a left-handed opener a possibility to line up against early left-handed bats like Ohtani and Freeman.
The Braves will continue to be without a pair of starters in right-hander Bryce Elder (knee) and left-hander Martin Perez (back).
Like Freeman before him, Olson has emerged as a Braves leader, along with Ronald Acuna Jr. Olson hit a team-best 41 home runs in the regular season and added another in the wild-card round. Harris hit 26 home runs in the regular season and Acuna added 20 homers and 21 steals.
“I think it’s just kind of going out there and playing our game and knowing that … we can compete with them and beat them,” said Braves catcher Drake Baldwin, an All-Star and 2025 NL Rookie of the Year who contributed 25 home runs.
–Doug Padilla, Field Level Media

item.title: [LAmag] Tarik Skubal, the Dodgers and the Price of October - LAmag
item.dc:creator: Camryn Rael
item.description: As the Dodgers look toward an October full of high-stakes games and another attempt to bring a World Series title back to Los Angeles, Tarik Skubal is looking a little farther ahead. After the postseason, the two-time American League Cy Young Award winner will become a free agent — and the Dodgers will have to decide how much they are willing to pay to keep him. Los Angeles acquired Skubal from the Detroit Tigers at the Aug. 2 trade deadline, giving up three prospects for one of baseball’s most
item.content:encoded:
As the Dodgers look toward an October full of high-stakes games and another attempt to bring a World Series title back to Los Angeles, Tarik Skubal is looking a little farther ahead. After the postseason, the two-time American League Cy Young Award winner will become a free agent — and the Dodgers will have to decide how much they are willing to pay to keep him.
Los Angeles acquired Skubal from the Detroit Tigers at the Aug. 2 trade deadline, giving up three prospects for one of baseball’s most accomplished starting pitchers. The Dodgers did not make the move simply to add another arm for the regular season. It was building toward October, where its goal is a third consecutive championship.
So far, the investment has paid off. Skubal posted a 2.61 ERA across 10 starts with Los Angeles and finished the regular season with seven scoreless innings against the San Francisco Giants. Now, the Dodgers are handing him the ball for Game 1 of the National League Division Series against the Atlanta Braves.
But Skubal’s October is unfolding alongside a much larger question: what happens when it ends?
Because the Dodgers acquired Skubal during the season, they did not acquire his long-term rights. He is set to enter free agency after the World Series, allowing him to negotiate with Los Angeles or any other team willing to meet his price. Players acquired in this way, shortly before free agency, are often described as “rentals” — players a team brings in for the remainder of a season with no guarantee they will return. For the Dodgers, the ideal return on that investment would be another championship. If Skubal helps deliver a third consecutive title, the prospects it gave up for a few months of his services could look like a worthwhile price.
That price could be among the largest ever for a pitcher. ESPN recently asked 27 MLB insiders to project Skubal’s next contract. Their estimates ranged from $176 million over four years to $500 million over 10 years, with an average projection of $355 million over eight years. Most of the predictions landed between $325 million and $400 million.
The clearest comparison for Dodgers fans is Yoshinobu Yamamoto. Before the 2024 season, Los Angeles signed him to a $325 million contract, setting the record for the largest guaranteed contract given to a pitcher in free agency. MLB now identifies that deal as the benchmark Skubal could surpass this offseason.
Skubal’s case for a larger contract is straightforward: he has won two consecutive Cy Young Awards and remains one of the most dominant pitchers in baseball. But there is risk in paying a 30-year-old pitcher hundreds of millions of dollars, particularly one with a history of elbow procedures. That combination — elite production and long-term uncertainty — will shape the bidding for him this winter.
Scroll to continue reading
And Skubal will not be navigating that market alone. His agent, Scott Boras, represents some of baseball’s highest-paid players and has negotiated several record-setting contracts. Boras will be responsible for helping Skubal determine not only how much he should seek, but what kind of contract makes the most sense — whether that means pursuing a shorter deal with a higher annual salary or building in options that give Skubal more control over his future. His strategy could play a significant role in determining where Skubal ultimately lands.
For now, though, Skubal’s value is being tested where the Dodgers need it most: October. His starts will give Los Angeles a closer look at what it has in the biggest games of the season — something the team will have to consider when deciding whether a long-term commitment makes sense.
But by the time the Dodgers’ season ends, the decision will no longer belong entirely to Los Angeles. Skubal and Boras will take that October experience into a market where multiple teams could be willing to pay for the same thing the Dodgers traded for in August: a top-of-the-rotation pitcher.
The Dodgers have Skubal through October. After that, they will have to decide what he is worth — and Skubal will have to decide whether their number is enough to keep him on the West Coast.

item.content:encoded:
Tigers fans will continue to be split on Tarik Skubal's legacy in Detroit, but there's one thing a lot of us can agree on: leaving Game 5 of the 2025 ALDS was pretty inexcusable.
At first blush, it was easy enough to sympathize with him. He'd thrown 99 pitches through six innings, and one man doesn't make a team. The Tigers' offense and bullpen failed them, and maybe it would've done them more harm than good to keep Skubal in the game if he was truly on his last legs. Maybe it was more of AJ Hinch's decision to take him out.
But every new development in the aftermath only made Tigers fans more and more sour on the situation. After that agonizing game, Skubal joked that he'd wondered if he could reenter in late innings. Fans' answer? Maybe you shouldn't have left so early in the first place, dude.
It got even worse when Skubal was notably self-critical after a six-inning, regular season start for the Dodgers shortly after the trade. The Tigers would've loved to see that kind of introspection from their ace after a postseason game rather than the shrug and "That's just baseball" response they got.
Skubal is reportedly set to be named the Dodgers' NLDS Game 1 starter. They'd better hope they don't get the version of Skubal the Tigers got in 2025.
Dodgers set to name Tarik Skubal NLDS Game 1 starter, but Tigers wounds are still fresh
Of course, it's incredibly likely that they don't. Skubal's in a walk year, and replicating that same kind of cavalier attitude about pitching in the pursuit of a championship wouldn't help him as a free agent.
But doesn't that kind of make it worse? That Skubal might only be ready to fully give it his all to set himself up to make a bigger buck in a few months' time, and only for one of the few teams that has the financial ability to keep him? The trade deadline was two months ago to the day, the Tigers' last stand in the ALDS almost exactly a year ago, but it all still stings.
Tigers fans can still think about the majority of Skubal's tenure in Detroit fondly while rooting heartily against him and the Dodgers throughout the duration of their postseason run. Go Braves, go Brewers or Padres, go whichever AL team they might see in the World Series.

item.content:encoded:
Now that the 2026 MLB regular season is done, Sony made one last ratings tweak for many of the players across the league on October 2. The October MLB The Show 26 ratings update saw Mookie Betts & Cade Smith rise to join the other Diamonds in the game.
The notable changes
Mookie Betts is back as a Diamond in MLB The Show 26. He and Cade Smith were the only two to move to Diamond status on October 2. Betts moved to 85 OVR after a strong final few weeks. Over his last 14 games, Betts slashed .316/.418/.632 with four home runs and 10 extra-base hits.
Smith, meanwhile, notched 41 saves and struck out 107 batters over 74 innings this season for the Guardians.
Fernando Tatis Jr. moved up three points between the last update and now. Tatis Jr., before the start of the playoffs, hit five home runs and nine extra-base hits in the last 15 games of the regular season for San Diego.
Elly De La Cruz, who had eight extra-base hits in the final two weeks, moved to 87 OVR, a +2 OVR increase. He moved there, along with NL Wild Card hero Michael Harris II.
As for who went down, Yandy Diaz and Jacob deGrom were both downgraded from Diamond status.

item.title: [New York Post] Dodgers saved by LA-based surgeon’s work on Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell
item.dc:creator: Dylan Hernandez
item.description: When Tarik Skubal was told a month into the season that he would have to get a bone chip removed from his left elbow, he expected the worst. item.content:encoded:
When Tarik Skubal was told a month into the season that he would have to get a bone chip removed from his left elbow, he expected the worst.
Skubal braced himself for the possibility of missing three months – maybe more.
“Crushed me,” he said.
Out of nowhere, Skubal received season-altering news.
Dr. Neal ElAttrache, the renowned Los Angeles-based surgeon who has operated on everyone from Kobe Bryant to Tom Brady, said he could perform a procedure using a camera the size of a pinhead. Because that camera, or scope, wouldn’t be any more invasive than, say, an injection, ElAttrache explained that his recovery time would be drastically reduced.
“I was like, ‘Yeah, absolutely,’” Skubal said. “I didn’t even need to hear anything else.”
There was one caveat: ElAttrache had never used the equipment on a high-profile athlete.
Nine days after the operation, Skubal was playing catch. About four weeks after that, he was pitching in a game.
But ElAttrache did more than save Skubal’s season.
He might have also saved the Dodgers’ season.
About two weeks after he operated on Skubal, ElAttrache performed a more complicated procedure using the NanoNeedle Scope 2.0 on Blake Snell.
Skubal was later traded by the Detroit Tigers to the Dodgers.
Without ElAttrache’s groundbreaking surgery, the Dodgers might not have two of their top three starting pitchers, and they certainly wouldn’t have the two two-time Cy Young Award winners pitching as well as they are now.
“Those solutions are a product of the genius of a doctor who has certainly proven to be Hall-of-Fame worthy,” said agent Scott Boras, who represents both pitchers.
Skubal estimated the surgery cost him only five starts. He pitched in 31 games in each of the last two seasons. He finished this season with 26.
“If it would have been three months,” Skubal said, “I would have missed 15, 16, 17 starts.”
That would have affected his performance.
As for Snell, he might not even be pitching now. Boras said that Snell could have been sidelined for six months if he’d undergone an operation using a traditional arthroscope.
Instead, Snell missed only half of that time and returned in the middle of August to make eight starts over the last two months of the regular season. In those eight starts, he was 4-0 with a 1.13 earned-run average.
“I just have more range,” Snell said. “Like, I can bend my elbow and throw stuff.”
Snell said his increased extension has improved his curveball by several orders of magnitude.
“The first time I threw the curveball, like, lightly, I was like, ‘Oh, it’s gonna be disgusting,’” Snell said.
Boras knew whom to call when he saw Skubal shaking his arm during a late-April start he made for the Tigers in Atlanta. Boras, who is based in Newport Beach, already had extensive history with ElAttrache, the team physician for the Dodgers and Rams. The influential agent estimates that he’s sent close to 1,000 of his clients to the celebrated doctor.
Unbeknownst to Boras, ElAttrache was pondering potential uses for a new surgical device on the market. The NanoNeedle 2.0 was equipped with a high-resolution camera that measured only 1.9 mm in diameter, or less than half the size of a standard arthroscope. Because it required smaller incisions, it would, in theory, result in less swelling and bleeding, which would accelerate the patient’s recovery time.
“I think it was useful especially because of the timing,” ElAttrache said.
Shutting down Skubal for three months would require him to build up his arm strength from scratch. His season could be lost.
ElAttrache wasn’t nervous about using the technology, as he’d experimented with it enough to where he’d developed a comfort with it.
“I’ve been using the scope in my practice for 35 years,” ElAttrache said. “It’s very natural for me. It’s not like I’m learning all new skills off the bat. It’s like an experienced pitcher learning a new pitch – not learning how to pitch.”
Skubal already trusted ElAttrache, who repaired his flexor tendon and guided his rehabilitation in 2022. He wasn’t reluctant to be Patient Zero.
“I was, like, ‘Hey, if you’re confident in it, I’m confident in it,’” Skubal said.
Skubal underwent surgery on May 6. He pitched his next game on June 13.
Snell’s case was more complicated. Not only did Snell have multiple bone chips floating around, he also had bone spurs on his elbow that had to be shaved down.
Snell had experience removing bone chips before with another surgeon, and it didn’t go well. When he returned from a 2019 cleanup while pitching for the Rays, he said, “My [velocity] was down and it hurt to throw.”
The discomfort was severe enough to make him consider a role change.
“I contemplated being a relief pitcher after that,” he said.
There were no such problems here.
As Boras recounted ElAttrache’s contributions in preparing his two clients for the upcoming postseason, he used the word “genius” to describe the doctor several times.
“He is very understanding of the players’ intentions and needs, in addition to those of the team,” Boras said.
The Dodgers will now enter the postseason two pitchers they might not have otherwise. A small camera and a doctor with the necessary know-how to use it are responsible.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Tigers Pitcher Acquired for Tarik Skubal Takes Apparent Shot at Dodgers
item.dc:creator: Ricardo Sandoval; Unknown
item.description: It's been two months since the Los Angeles Dodgers shocked the baseball world, trading for two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal. The Dodgers were always viewed as the frontrunners to trade for the southpaw pitcher; however, it was still hard to believe when it actually happened. With the Dodgers' postseason approaching, Skubal is poised to play a vital role in the team's quest for a three-peat. As for Skubal's former team, the Detroit Tigers, they're watching the postseason from home. The Tiger
item.content:encoded:
It's been two months since the Los Angeles Dodgers shocked the baseball world, trading for two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal.
The Dodgers were always viewed as the frontrunners to trade for the southpaw pitcher; however, it was still hard to believe when it actually happened.
With the Dodgers' postseason approaching, Skubal is poised to play a vital role in the team's quest for a three-peat. As for Skubal's former team, the Detroit Tigers, they're watching the postseason from home.
The Tigers received what they believed was the best package for Skubal. Detroit acquired outfielder Zyhir Hope and right-handed pitchers Brady Smith and River Ryan.
The Dodgers added an ace they hope they can lock up after the 2026 season, and the Tigers retooled their farm system with high-upside talent.
Los Angeles came out as the clear winners in the trade in present times, but Ryan is doing his best to ensure the Tigers come out as the winner when all is said and done.
On top of that, he took a subtle shot at the Dodgers while discussing his transition to the Tigers organization.
“I think the transition, as far as being traded on the injured list and then switching to a whole other organization and continuing through that process, I think Detroit made it really easy," Ryan said in a recent conversation with Just Baseball. "I think it was definitely a lot more hands-on with the Detroit organization. I feel like there was a lot more care involved, which was fantastic."
“They are being really involved in the day-to-day with me,” he added. “They’re all watching my outings, my bullpens. I mean, that’s really it. They’re just really trying to be as involved as they can on a day-to-day basis.”
Ryan also said the transition from Los Angeles to Detroit was pretty easy, since he's been traded before.
“I think since I’ve been through the trading process before, I kind of knew what to expect,” Ryan said. “Transitioning over to another team, meeting all new people, becoming acquainted with everybody. That was pretty easy because I’ve been through it before and I had a reference."
How Did River Ryan’s Dodgers Tenure Unfold?
Ryan was supposed to be a standout pitcher for the Dodgers. Unfortunately for him, his time in Los Angeles was riddled with injuries.
He missed the entire 2025 season recovering from Tommy John surgery and later dealt with minor setbacks like a hamstring issue, prompting the Dodgers to be extremely cautious with his workload.
Ryan, 28, will now do his best to pan out in the big leagues with the Tigers. He made two starts with the Tigers in late-September, alloiwng two runs over 4.1 innings with six strikeouts.

Ricardo Sandoval is a freelance writer with On SI. He is a graduate of California State University, Northridge, and specializes in sports writing, particularly in MLB, NBA and NFL. He previously served as an Associate Editor for Dodgers Nation and has worked with Newsweek and The Sporting News.

item.title: [yardbarker.com] Dodgers NLDS Notes: Edwin Díaz, Edgardo Henriquez & Starting Rotation
item.dc:creator: Matthew Moreno
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers earned the benefit of a postseason bye and now are reaping the full benefit as the Philadelphia Phillies staved off elimination to force the Atlanta Braves to a winner-take-all Game 3 in their Wild Card Series matchup. The winner advances to face the Dodgers in the National League Division Series, which begins Saturday at Dodger Stadium. The start for time for Game 1 has not yet been decided as it hinges on whether or not the San Diego Padres or Chicago Cubs reach the NLD
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers earned the benefit of a postseason bye and now are reaping the full benefit as the Philadelphia Phillies staved off elimination to force the Atlanta Braves to a winner-take-all Game 3 in their Wild Card Series matchup.
The winner advances to face the Dodgers in the National League Division Series, which begins Saturday at Dodger Stadium. The start for time for Game 1 has not yet been decided as it hinges on whether or not the San Diego Padres or Chicago Cubs reach the NLDS to play the Milwaukee Brewers.
In the meantime, the Dodgers are spending the rest of the week going through workouts and simulated games, much like their approach in 2024 that proved beneficial.
The Dodgers avoiding the Wild Card Series this year has proven beneficial for multiple players dealing with an injury, including Edgardo Henriquez.
He missed the final two weeks because of lower back discomfort but has made steady progress in his recovery and is on track for the NLDS.
“We’ll get him some work this week. He’s trending really well at this point,” Dodgers general manager Brandon Gomes said on Tuesday. “His last live BP went well, he’s responding positively after he throws and isn’t feeling any lingering discomfort.
“We’ve still got a few steps to go, but if that all goes well, then yeah, the expectation is he’ll be on the roster.”
Elsewhere in the Dodgers bullpen, Edwin Díaz finished the regular season on a high note after returning from a stint on the 15-day injured list because of a neck issue.
“I don’t know if we could have asked much more out of Edwin. I think it was, like, a 50-plus percent strikeout rate when he came back,” Gomes noted. “Felt like each outing was more and more sharp, and looking more like himself.
“Feels like he’s in a great place right now, stuff out of hand is as good as it’s been all year, and we know that he has pitched in the hottest of hot games in the past, and in any role, especially in the postseason. He’s looked great and glad that he’s in the position that he’s in and was able to bounce back after the IL stint.”
Díaz threw five scoreless innings, allowed just one hit and one walk while collecting nine strikeouts across five appearances upon getting activated Sept. 18. While Gomes projected confidence, what may still be different for Díaz is he’s not relied upon as the primary closer.
Even without Shohei Ohtani pitching, the Dodgers are heading into the playoffs with a formidable starting rotation that consists of Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow. What order they will pitch in has not yet been decided.
Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said the team would not set their NLDS rotation until Thursday, at which point they would know whether the Braves or Phillies advanced.
“I say that because just trying to figure out opponent and the schedule going forward, not sure about game times and things like that. We’re having conversations but we’re not definitive yet,” Roberts explained.
“I think opponent certainly should matter, could matter. Talking to Mark Prior about where guys are at. To be honest, we could really put all four guys in a hat and run them out there. But I think there is going to be more thought behind it. We don’t need to make a decision right now, so really just trying to be clear and talk through it.”
Last year the Dodgers almost exclusively used Snell (Wild Card, NL Championship Series and World Series) as their Game 1 starter. Ohtani started against the Phillies in the opener of the NLDS.
One change from the 2025 postseason is Glasnow’s first appearance likely won’t come out of the bullpen during the NLDS due in part to a different schedule.

item.title: [heavy.com] Why David Stearns’ Pitching Philosophy Stands Between the Mets and Tarik Skubal
item.dc:creator: Terrance Biggs
item.description: New York Mets owner Steve Cohen is the richest in the MLB. He’s spent at least a billion dollars in contracts to bring a World Series trophy back to Queens. However, his money did nothing but return misery and hopelessness. Unlike his predecessors, the Wilpons, Cohen is more than eager to open his wallet and continue trying to bring talent to Flushing. Meanwhile, David Stearns, the president of baseball operations, faces criticism from both media and fans for free agent signings that have not be
item.content:encoded:
New York Mets owner Steve Cohen is the richest in the MLB. He’s spent at least a billion dollars in contracts to bring a World Series trophy back to Queens. However, his money did nothing but return misery and hopelessness. Unlike his predecessors, the Wilpons, Cohen is more than eager to open his wallet and continue trying to bring talent to Flushing.
Meanwhile, David Stearns, the president of baseball operations, faces criticism from both media and fans for free agent signings that have not been successful. With the exception of Juan Soto, who continues to excel, Stearns’ eye for talent seems to have suffered from astigmatism, where he cannot judge the proximity of the roster to becoming a winning one.
Yet, some believe that lefthander Tarik Skubal, in the estimation of many, could be the one to lead the Mets back to the playoffs. However, considering Stearns’ approach, the deal looks like a long shot. Stearns, in his season postmortem, discussed the need for starting pitching.
“I do think it is necessary for us to add to our rotation,” Stearns said. “We can do that in a variety of different ways. We’ve talked about this plenty before—you’d always love to add to the top of your rotation; any team would love to do that. Over the long term, what we need to do is develop pitchers at the top of our rotation, and I think we are proving we can do that, and we’ll continue to do that.”
On Baseball Night in New York, @chelsea_janes says “call me crazy” but she’d rather have two good starters opposed to getting just Tarik Skubal pic.twitter.com/STB6i2PTe2
— SNY Mets (@SNY_Mets) September 28, 2026
Making the Case
First, Skubal is a southpaw that the Mets need to break up their righty-dominant rotation. More importantly, his 2.72 ERA & 0.96 WHIP suggest that he continues to dominate pitchers, even after changing leads and settling into the Los Angeles Dodgers pressure cooker.
It makes sense to bring in an elite lefty to minimize the impact of Bryce Harper, Pete Crow-Armstrong, Kyle Schwarber, and Shohei Ohtani. Additionally, Skubal’s presence would also take the pressure off a bullpen that sorely needs a frontline starter to pitch into the seventh inning. Freddy Peralta was supposed to be the one, but he often struggled to escape the fifth.
Tarik Skubal has 10 Ks through 6 scoreless innings! pic.twitter.com/LOWMtaLuIf
— MLB (@MLB) September 26, 2026
Against the Grain
Stearns, during his time with Milwaukee, built his rosters on a mix of young talent, under-contract control, and not paying pitchers long-term. As a result, when news of Peralta sought a nine-year extension, his days in New York became shorter. Stearns, to his credit, continues to build a farm system that produces young talent.
Skubal presents a departure from all of that. First, he will command at least $300 million in a long-term contract. Next, Stesarns wants the rotation to still have room for the younger pitchers like Christian Scott, Nolan McLean, Zac Thornton, and eventually Jonah Tong. To sign Skubal, Stearns would need to completely change how he fundamentally views pitching, and that does not seem to be the case at all.
Danny Abriano of SNY outlined the perils of signing a veteran pitcher long-term.
“For every long-term, big-money deal to a pitcher 29 or older that works out (Max Scherzer’s seven-year deal with the Nationals looks incredible in retrospect, and the Yankees‘ deal for Max Fried is aging well), you can point to a whole bunch that didn’t or currently aren’t (Patrick Corbin, Jacob deGrom, Jordan Zimmermann, Felix Hernandez, and Corbin Burnes).”
Scherzer and Fried appear to be the few exceptions to the rule. Otherwise, it’s a dice roll on what type of arm you will get. On top of that, Skubal already underwent a medical procedure this season.
Mets fans see Skubal as their ticket to the playoffs. Similarly, some media do. However, the Mets, despite their abundant supply of cash, could look to other avenues.

item.title: [Dodgers Way] Projecting the Dodgers' NLDS roster with Josue De Paula, bench shuffle
item.dc:creator: Katrina Stebbins
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers get to kick back and watch as eight teams duke it out to move on to their respective League Division Series this week. The Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies will go head-to-head in the NL Wild Card Series before one of them moves on to try and topple LA. One would think that this Dodgers team would have everything buttoned up well ahead of the NLDS, but there are still a couple of key questions to be answered. Projecting the Dodgers' NLDS roster with Josue De Paula
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers get to kick back and watch as eight teams duke it out to move on to their respective League Division Series this week. The Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies will go head-to-head in the NL Wild Card Series before one of them moves on to try and topple LA.
One would think that this Dodgers team would have everything buttoned up well ahead of the NLDS, but there are still a couple of key questions to be answered.
Projecting the Dodgers' NLDS roster with Josue De Paula called upon
Catchers (2): Will Smith, Hunter Feduccia
For some reason, the Dodgers decided to carry three catchers on their Wild Card and NLDS rosters last year — Smith, Dalton Rushing, and Ben Rortvedt — but adjusted ahead of the NLCS by shedding Rushing, who received just one at-bat in the NLDS but otherwise rode the bench.
Rortvedt didn't get a start or even substitution after Game 2 of the NLDS with Smith slowly coming back from injury at the beginning of the postseason. Feduccia figures to play a similar break-glass-in-case-of-emergency role. As a lefty, he could get a start and then an early pull depending on matchups but, barring disaster, it's mostly going to be Smith's show.
Designated hitters (2): Shohei Ohtani, Josue De Paula
The Dodgers clearly want to find a way to bring De Paula with them in October, even if only as a lingering threat on their bench. They're reportedly not entertaining putting him in the outfield at all, and it's not hard to see why. Even if they're confident they'll be able to fix his defense in time, they can't afford any leakage in the postseason.
Ohtani is still shaking off the cobwebs from his 15-day IL stint. He picked up a few hits with promising exit velocity in his return against the San Diego Padres and later against the San Francisco Giants, but there are still question marks around what version of him we might see this postseason.
Infielders (6): Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts, Tommy Edman, Max Muncy, Miguel Rojas, Kiké Hernández
A notable exclusion here is Hyeseong Kim. Although he's in the running to get a spot on the bench and exclusively come into games to pinch-run or for reassurances on defense, there's still a chance he doesn't make the roster if the Dodgers are set on carrying 13 pitchers. Edman and Hernández, though lacking the same speed as Kim, can still offer the same defensive versatility.
Outfielders (3): Andy Pages, Kyle Tucker, Teoscar Hernández
Pages might've found himself in the same boat as Ohtani, but he announced his return to the Dodgers after a month-long IL stint in a big way, hitting .333 with a 1.180 OPS, two homers, and five RBI against the Padres and Giants. No doubt Dave Roberts and Andrew Friedman breathed a massive sigh of relief.
Alex Call will be the odd man out. He was on all four of LA's playoff rosters last year and received sporadic appearances throughout the month, but that was when Michael Conforto was still on the payroll. Tucker and Hernández have certainly had their ups-and-downs this season, but the Dodgers would never seriously consider leaving them out.
Starters (4): Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell, Tarik Skubal, Tyler Glasnow
There's not much to say about what's probably the best rotation going into the postseason. Snell and Glasnow have both battled injury this season but came back when the Dodgers needed them most. It might be too much to ask that any of Yamamoto, Snell, or Glasnow replicate their dominance from last year, but they'll certainly try.
Relievers: (9): Tanner Scott, Roki Sasaki, Alex Vesia, Evan Phillips, Brock Stewart, Justin Wrobleski, Edwin Díaz, Kris Bubic, Edgardo Henriquez
Just like 2025, this is where things get dicey. The Dodgers' bullpen isn't quite as banged up or as unreliable as they were last year, but they're not the air-tight, bulletproof coterie that their combined salaries suggest they should be. Henriquez will be coming straight off of the IL to rejoin the team in the NLDS, and Díaz, Sasaki, and Scott are all woefully unpredictable.
There is some thought that the Dodgers might carry eight relievers instead of nine, to free up a spot on the position player side for a guy like Kim. In this scenario, we'll stick with them taking nine. If not, Bubic is the most obvious cut. Last one in, first one out.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Mets should make all-out Tarik Skubal pursuit, but it could take a philosophical shift
item.dc:creator: Danny Abriano
item.description: As the Mets enter the offseason, they'll be facing a familiar challenge: put together a team that can get them back to the playoffs for the first time since 2024. David Stearns and the front office failed in that regard last offseason, due in part to the drastic changes that were made to the roster and coaching staff. There were other things at play, including long-term injuries to Francisco Lindor and Clay Holmes, some worst-case scenarios playing out, and an over-reliance on bounce backs. This
item.content:encoded:
As the Mets enter the offseason, they'll be facing a familiar challenge: put together a team that can get them back to the playoffs for the first time since 2024.
David Stearns and the front office failed in that regard last offseason, due in part to the drastic changes that were made to the roster and coaching staff. There were other things at play, including long-term injuries to Francisco Lindor and Clay Holmes, some worst-case scenarios playing out, and an over-reliance on bounce backs.
This time around, the Mets will almost certainly have much less turnover, but that doesn't mean the overall result in 2026 wasn't an abject failure.
New York had a 34-31 record after the All-Star break, which was a big improvement after things spun out of control in the first half and led to a trade deadline sell-off.
But the most important developments for the Mets after their dismal start? The emergence of Carson Benge and A.J. Ewing, the impressive return of Christian Scott, the moxie and performance of Zac Thornton, and some good late-season signs from Jonah Tong.
The above should give the Mets confidence that they're in solid shape when it comes to their lineup and a chunk of the starting rotation. They have an emerging young core to complement their more established stars, and potentially have high-upside players coming soon from the upper levels of the minors. But serious help is still needed this winter.
Specifically, the Mets need to add external help at first base, address the DH spot, bolster the bullpen with multiple new arms (including a back end option), and -- most importantly -- find a pitcher who profiles at the very top of the rotation.
In both 2025 and 2026, the Mets were done in, due in large part to not having enough starting pitching depth. And it can be argued that they left themselves short one legitimate starter both times. That can't happen again, so New York should be focused on pairing a new prospective ace with another addition who profiles in the middle or back of the rotation.
About that ace ... it's not difficult to figure out that it should be Tarik Skubal.
In one of the weakest free agent classes in recent memory, Skubal stands out even more than he ordinarily would.
Fresh off back-to-back Cy Young awards, the 29-year-old Skubal posted a 2.72 ERA (2.51 FIP) and 0.96 WHIP while walking just 1.5 per nine innings and striking out 186 batters in 158.2 innings in 2026.
Skubal's season was briefly interrupted by NanoScope surgery on his pitching elbow that kept him out of action from April 30 through June 13. But he continued to be dominant upon his return. After having a 2.70 ERA (2.11 FIP) over his first seven starts, Skubal had a 2.73 ERA (2.66 FIP) in the 19 starts he made post-surgery, with 10 of them coming after he was dealt to the Dodgers at the trade deadline.
During Stearns' end-of-season news conference on Monday at Citi Field, he was asked multiple times about the Mets' offseason plan for adding pitching, but unsurprisingly didn't offer much when asked in a roundabout way about a possible Skubal pursuit.
"I do think it is necessary for us to add to our rotation," Stearns said. "We can do that in a variety of different ways. We've talked about this plenty before -- you'd always love to add to the top of your rotation, any team would love to do that -- over the long term, what we need to do is develop pitchers at the top of our rotation, and I think we are proving we can do that, and we'll continue to do that."
While Stearns refused to make any declarations about the type of pitcher the Mets would go after, it is pointless to read into that.
For one, Skubal is still under contract with the Dodgers, and no executive is going to talk about going after a player who is on another team.
Second, and even more importantly, no exec is going to tip his or her hand entirely and risk wrecking leverage ahead of possible negotiations.
While Stearns (smartly) won't say it, I will: The Mets should make Skubal the centerpiece of their offseason plan, using the resources at their disposal to add one of the most talented pitchers in the sport to slot in front of Nolan McLean.
The Mets' biggest need this offseason is at the top of their rotation, with Skubal a nearly perfect way to fill that need. And Skubal will cost only money, since the midseason trade from Detroit to Los Angeles makes him ineligible for a qualifying offer and the draft pick compensation it would've required from any team that signed him.
When discussing Skubal and the Mets, it's obviously instructive to consider Stearns' philosophy when it comes to signing pitchers to long-term deals. Specifically, he has not shown much interest in signing pitchers in their late-20s or 30s to those kind of pacts -- and that philosophy is generally a valid one.
For every long-term, big-money deal to a pitcher 29 or older that works out (Max Scherzer's seven-year deal with the Nationals looks incredible in retrospect, and the Yankees' deal for Max Fried is aging well), you can point to a whole bunch that didn't or currently aren't (Patrick Corbin, Jacob deGrom, Jordan Zimmermann, Felix Hernandez, Corbin Burnes).
As far as how Stearns has operated in the past, it's fair to throw what he did in Milwaukee out the window given the payroll constraints he was working under.
But except for a serious pursuit of then-25-year-old Yoshinobu Yamamoto ahead of the 2024 season, Stearns' main forays into the free agent starting pitching market with the Mets have been measured:
Sean Manaea: Three years, $75 million
Clay Holmes: Three years, $38 million
Frankie Montas: Two years, $34 million
Luis Severino: One year, $13 million
Griffin Canning: One year, $4.25 million
Of those signings, Holmes was the biggest success as the Mets turned him back into a starter after he spent years in relief. But that success resulted in Holmes being set to opt out after the second season of his contract, which led to New York trading him at the deadline.
During his time leading the Mets' baseball operations, Stearns has been reluctant to offer deals to starting pitchers (except Yamamoto) that exceed three years. When that is your philosophy, the risk is obviously lower. But sometimes a calculated risk is needed.
When it comes to Skubal, there is risk. In addition to the minor surgery he had this season, Skubal underwent flexor tendon surgery in 2022 and had Tommy John surgery in 2017.
Skubal is also likely to receive the biggest deal ever for a starting pitcher when it comes to average annual value. Maybe his age (30 when next season begins) and yearly value of his deal will make the years easier to stomach, but something like $400 million for eight years is easy to imagine.
There's also the looming lockout and new CBA to consider.
While it's difficult to envision the players caving on a hard salary cap, it's fair to believe the new CBA will include stiffer penalties for teams that exceed the luxury tax thresholds.
But even after considering all of that, it's still reasonable to conclude that the Mets should go after Skubal with gusto -- that he should be the exception to Stearns' rule, maybe with a slight nudge from owner Steve Cohen.
Things could always go sideways, as they often do with long-term deals for older starting pitchers. But there's no reason to think Skubal won't be exceptional for the first half of any deal he signs, which would also theoretically line up with a World Series window the Mets will hope to be entering.
When you look at Skubal, who combines one of the best arsenals in baseball with perhaps the best command in baseball (and whose metrics look like this), the biggest risk for the Mets would be not going all-in on him.

item.title: [heavy.com] Dodgers Linked to Tarik Skubal As Former GM Reveals Potential Price Tag
item.dc:creator: Maria Aldrich
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers rattled the MLB world after they acquired southpaw Tarik Skubal back in August.
